entry.sum: A differential $k$-form is an object that can be integrated over $k$-dimensional pieces of space: at each point it is an alternating $k$-linear function of tangent vectors, written in coordinates as a combination of wedge products such as $f\,dx\wedge dy$. The exterior derivative $d$ turns $k$-forms into $(k+1)$-forms, satisfies $d\circ d=0$, and the general Stokes theorem $\int_M d\omega=\int_{\partial M}\omega$ contains the fundamental theorem of calculus and the theorems of Green, Stokes and Gauss as special cases.
entry.why: Forms give one coordinate-free language for integration on curves, surfaces and manifolds, in which gradient, curl and divergence become a single operator $d$; Maxwell's equations, de Rham cohomology and the Gauss–Bonnet theorem are all written in it.

links.note: Closed forms modulo exact forms give de Rham cohomology, a topological invariant: the angle form on the punctured plane is closed but not exact precisely because the plane has a hole.
For holomorphic $f$ the 1-form $f\,dz$ is closed, so Cauchy's integral theorem is the two-dimensional Stokes theorem applied to $f\,dz$.

Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds
Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis

blocks.body:
Vector calculus ends with a collection of integral theorems that look alike but are stated separately: the fundamental theorem of calculus, Green's theorem in the plane, the Kelvin–Stokes theorem for surfaces and the divergence theorem for solids (see [[vector-calculus]]). Each says that integrating some kind of derivative over a region equals integrating the original object over the boundary of the region. Differential forms are the objects that make this a single statement.

The idea is to stop integrating functions and start integrating things that already know how to measure. A $1$-form eats a small arrow and returns a number, so it can be summed along a curve. A $2$-form eats two small arrows and returns a signed area, so it can be summed over a surface. One derivative $d$ acts on all of them, and one theorem, $\int_M d\omega=\int_{\partial M}\omega$, covers every case.

blocks.title: Things you integrate along curves
blocks.body:
In the plane, $dx$ is the function that takes a vector $v=(v_1,v_2)$ and returns its first component $v_1$; similarly $dy(v)=v_2$. A $1$-form is an expression $\omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy$ with smooth functions $P,Q$; at the point $p$ it sends $v$ to $P(p)v_1+Q(p)v_2$.

To integrate $\omega$ along a curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}^2$, chop the curve into tiny steps. On each step the curve moves by approximately the velocity $\gamma'(t)\,\Delta t$, and $\omega$ assigns that step the number $\omega_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t))\,\Delta t$. Adding up and refining gives
$$\int_\gamma \omega=\int_a^b \Big(P(\gamma(t))\,x'(t)+Q(\gamma(t))\,y'(t)\Big)\,dt,$$
which is exactly the line integral of the vector field $(P,Q)$. For example, with $\omega=-y\,dx+x\,dy$ and the unit circle $\gamma(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)$, $0\le t\le 2\pi$, the integrand is $\sin^2t+\cos^2t=1$ and $\int_\gamma\omega=2\pi$.

Two features are already visible. The answer does not depend on how fast we traverse the curve, only on its direction: reversing the direction flips the sign. And the integrand needed no lengths or angles, only the derivative of the parametrisation. These two features, orientation and independence from any metric, persist in every dimension.

blocks.title: Wedge products: signed areas and volumes
blocks.body:
To integrate over surfaces we need something that eats two vectors. Define
$$(dx\wedge dy)(v,w)=v_1w_2-v_2w_1=\det\begin{pmatrix}v_1&w_1\\ v_2&w_2\end{pmatrix},$$
the signed area of the parallelogram spanned by the projections of $v$ and $w$ to the $xy$-plane. Swapping $v$ and $w$ flips the sign, so $dy\wedge dx=-dx\wedge dy$, and in particular $dx\wedge dx=0$. In general, for $1$-forms $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k$ the product $\alpha_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\alpha_k$ sends $(v_1,\dots,v_k)$ to $\det[\alpha_i(v_j)]$. This is the exterior algebra of [[tensor-products]], applied to the dual of each tangent space.

In $\mathbb{R}^n$ write $dx_I=dx_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_{i_k}$ for an increasing multi-index $I=(i_1< \dots< i_k)$. Every alternating $k$-linear form on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a unique combination of these, so the space of such forms has dimension $\binom nk$. In $\mathbb{R}^3$ that gives dimensions $1,3,3,1$ for $k=0,1,2,3$: functions, objects like $P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz$, objects like $A\,dy\wedge dz+B\,dz\wedge dx+C\,dx\wedge dy$, and multiples of $dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$. That count, three and three, is why vector calculus can get away with using vector fields for both $1$-forms and $2$-forms.

The determinant hidden inside the wedge product is what makes the change-of-variables formula of [[multiple-integrals]] automatic. In polar coordinates $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$ we have $dx=\cos\theta\,dr-r\sin\theta\,d\theta$ and $dy=\sin\theta\,dr+r\cos\theta\,d\theta$. Multiplying out and using $dr\wedge dr=d\theta\wedge d\theta=0$,
$$dx\wedge dy=(r\cos^2\theta+r\sin^2\theta)\,dr\wedge d\theta=r\,dr\wedge d\theta.$$
The Jacobian factor $r$ appears without being asked for.

blocks.title: Differential form
blocks.body:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be open. A differential $k$-form on $U$ is an expression
$$\omega=\sum_{I}f_I\,dx_I,$$
summed over increasing multi-indices $I$ of length $k$, with smooth functions $f_I:U\to\mathbb{R}$. At each point $p$ it is the alternating $k$-linear map $(v_1,\dots,v_k)\mapsto\sum_I f_I(p)\,dx_I(v_1,\dots,v_k)$. A $0$-form is a smooth function. The wedge product of forms is computed by multiplying out and using $dx_i\wedge dx_j=-dx_j\wedge dx_i$; for a $k$-form $\alpha$ and an $l$-form $\beta$ one gets $\beta\wedge\alpha=(-1)^{kl}\alpha\wedge\beta$.

Meaning: a $k$-form is a smoothly varying rule for measuring oriented $k$-dimensional volume, ready to be integrated over $k$-dimensional objects.

blocks.title: Exterior derivative
blocks.body:
For a function $f$, $df=\sum_{j=1}^n \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_j}\,dx_j$. For a $k$-form $\omega=\sum_I f_I\,dx_I$,
$$d\omega=\sum_I df_I\wedge dx_I=\sum_I\sum_{j=1}^n\frac{\partial f_I}{\partial x_j}\,dx_j\wedge dx_I .$$
It is linear and satisfies the Leibniz rule $d(\alpha\wedge\beta)=d\alpha\wedge\beta+(-1)^k\alpha\wedge d\beta$ for a $k$-form $\alpha$.

Meaning: $d\omega$ measures how $\omega$ fails to cancel around the boundary of a tiny $(k+1)$-dimensional box, which is exactly what the Stokes theorem turns into a global statement.

blocks.title: d squared is zero
blocks.body: For every smooth $k$-form $\omega$ on an open set of $\mathbb{R}^n$, $d(d\omega)=0$.

blocks.title: Proof that d∘d = 0
blocks.body:
By linearity it suffices to take $\omega=f\,dx_I$. Then $d\omega=\sum_j \partial_j f\,dx_j\wedge dx_I$, and since $d(dx_I)=0$ (its coefficient is the constant $1$),
$$d(d\omega)=\sum_{i,j}\partial_i\partial_j f\;dx_i\wedge dx_j\wedge dx_I .$$
The terms with $i=j$ vanish because $dx_i\wedge dx_i=0$. The terms with $i\ne j$ come in pairs $(i,j)$ and $(j,i)$; their coefficients $\partial_i\partial_jf$ and $\partial_j\partial_if$ are equal by the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives for smooth functions (see [[partial-derivatives]]), while $dx_j\wedge dx_i=-dx_i\wedge dx_j$. So each pair cancels and $d(d\omega)=0$.

blocks.title: The dictionary with vector calculus
blocks.body:
In $\mathbb{R}^3$ match $1$-forms with vector fields by $F=(F_1,F_2,F_3)\leftrightarrow F_1\,dx+F_2\,dy+F_3\,dz$, and $2$-forms with vector fields by $G\leftrightarrow G_1\,dy\wedge dz+G_2\,dz\wedge dx+G_3\,dx\wedge dy$. Direct computation from the definition gives:

1. For a function $f$, $df$ corresponds to $\nabla f$.
2. For a $1$-form, $d(F_1\,dx+F_2\,dy+F_3\,dz)$ corresponds to $\operatorname{curl}F$. For instance the $dy\wedge dz$ coefficient is $\partial_yF_3-\partial_zF_2$.
3. For a $2$-form, $$d(G_1\,dy\wedge dz+G_2\,dz\wedge dx+G_3\,dx\wedge dy)=(\partial_xG_1+\partial_yG_2+\partial_zG_3)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$$, the divergence.

Under this dictionary $d\circ d=0$ becomes the two identities $\operatorname{curl}(\nabla f)=0$ and $\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}F)=0$. In the plane, $d(P\,dx+Q\,dy)=(\partial_xQ-\partial_yP)\,dx\wedge dy$, the integrand of Green's theorem.

A form with $d\omega=0$ is called closed; a form with $\omega=d\eta$ for some $\eta$ is called exact. By $d\circ d=0$, exact forms are closed. Whether closed forms are exact depends on the shape of the domain, as the example "Closed but not exact" shows.

blocks.title: Pullback, orientation and integration
blocks.body:
If $\varphi:V\to U$ is smooth, with $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m$, the pullback $\varphi^*\omega$ is the form on $V$ obtained by substituting $x=\varphi(u)$: replace each coefficient $f(x)$ by $f(\varphi(u))$ and each $dx_i$ by $d\varphi_i=\sum_j \partial_{u_j}\varphi_i\,du_j$. The polar computation above was the pullback of $dx\wedge dy$. Pullback respects wedge products and commutes with the derivative: $d(\varphi^*\omega)=\varphi^*(d\omega)$.

Integration is defined by pulling back to a box. On a box $B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^k$ with its standard orientation, $\int_B f\,du_1\wedge\cdots\wedge du_k=\int_B f\,du_1\cdots du_k$, an ordinary multiple integral. For a parametrised $k$-dimensional piece $\varphi:B\to\mathbb{R}^n$, define $\int_\varphi\omega=\int_B\varphi^*\omega$. If $\psi$ is an orientation-preserving reparametrisation (positive Jacobian determinant), the change-of-variables formula shows that the answer is unchanged; if the Jacobian determinant is negative the sign flips. So a $k$-form can be integrated over any oriented $k$-dimensional manifold, by cutting it into parametrised pieces, or more cleanly with a partition of unity, as on [[smooth-manifolds]].

The boundary $\partial M$ of an oriented manifold with boundary gets the induced orientation: a basis $(v_1,\dots,v_{k-1})$ of the tangent space of $\partial M$ is positive if (outward normal, $v_1,\dots,v_{k-1}$) is positive for $M$. For a region in the plane this means the boundary is traversed with the region on the left.

blocks.title: The general Stokes theorem
blocks.body:
Let $M$ be an oriented smooth $k$-dimensional manifold with boundary, with $\partial M$ carrying the induced orientation, and let $\omega$ be a smooth $(k-1)$-form on $M$ with compact support. Then
$$\int_M d\omega=\int_{\partial M}\omega .$$
If $\partial M=\varnothing$ the right side is $0$. The same identity holds for a smooth singular $k$-chain $c$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$: $\int_c d\omega=\int_{\partial c}\omega$.

blocks.title: Proof for a cube, and how the general case follows
blocks.body:
Let $I^k=[0,1]^k$ with its standard orientation. For $j=1,\dots,k$ and $\alpha\in\{0,1\}$ let the face map $\iota_{j,\alpha}:I^{k-1}\to I^k$ insert $\alpha$ as the $j$-th coordinate, and define the oriented boundary $\partial I^k=\sum_{j,\alpha}(-1)^{j+\alpha}\iota_{j,\alpha}$. (For $k=2$ this is the square traversed counterclockwise.)

By linearity we may take $\omega=f\,dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\widehat{dx_i}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_k$, where the hat means that $dx_i$ is omitted. In $d\omega$ only $\partial_if\,dx_i$ survives the wedge with the remaining $dx$'s, and moving $dx_i$ into position $i$ past $i-1$ factors gives
$$d\omega=(-1)^{i-1}\,\partial_if\;dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_k .$$
Integrate first in $x_i$ using the one-variable fundamental theorem of calculus:
$$\int_{I^k}d\omega=(-1)^{i-1}\int_{I^{k-1}}\Big(f|_{x_i=1}-f|_{x_i=0}\Big)\,dx_1\cdots\widehat{dx_i}\cdots dx_k .$$
Now the boundary. On a face with $j\ne i$ the coordinate $x_j$ is constant, so $\iota_{j,\alpha}^*dx_j=0$; since $dx_j$ occurs in $\omega$, the pullback vanishes. On the faces $j=i$ the pullback is $f|_{x_i=\alpha}\,dt_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dt_{k-1}$. Hence
$$\int_{\partial I^k}\omega=(-1)^{i+1}\int f|_{x_i=1}+(-1)^{i}\int f|_{x_i=0},$$
which is the same expression. So the theorem holds for the cube.

For a singular cube, a smooth map $c=\varphi:I^k\to\mathbb{R}^n$ with $\partial c=\sum_{j,\alpha}(-1)^{j+\alpha}\varphi\circ\iota_{j,\alpha}$, the result follows by pulling back, since $$\int_c d\omega=\int_{I^k}\varphi^*d\omega=\int_{I^k}d(\varphi^*\omega)=\int_{\partial I^k}\varphi^*\omega=\int_{\partial c}\omega$$, and for chains by adding. For a manifold one writes $\omega$ as a finite sum of forms supported in coordinate charts using a partition of unity, applies the cube case (or a half-cube case at the boundary) in each chart, and adds; this last step is standard bookkeeping and is done carefully in Lee, chapter 16.

blocks.title: Green's theorem as a special case
blocks.body: Let $D$ be the closed unit disc and $\omega=-y\,dx+x\,dy$. Compute $\int_D d\omega$ and $\int_{\partial D}\omega$ separately and check that they agree. What does this say about area?
blocks.solution:
First, $d\omega=d(-y)\wedge dx+dx\wedge dy=-dy\wedge dx+dx\wedge dy=2\,dx\wedge dy$. So $\int_Dd\omega=2\cdot\operatorname{area}(D)=2\pi$.

The boundary circle with the induced orientation is traversed counterclockwise, $\gamma(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)$. Pulling back, $\gamma^*\omega=(-\sin t)(-\sin t\,dt)+\cos t(\cos t\,dt)=dt$, so $\int_{\partial D}\omega=\int_0^{2\pi}dt=2\pi$. The two sides agree.

The same computation for any region $R$ with piecewise smooth boundary gives the area formula $\operatorname{area}(R)=\tfrac12\oint_{\partial R}(x\,dy-y\,dx)$. This is the principle behind the planimeter, a mechanical instrument that measures area by tracing the boundary.

blocks.title: Flux through the sphere
blocks.body: Let $\omega=x\,dy\wedge dz+y\,dz\wedge dx+z\,dx\wedge dy$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$ and let $S$ be the unit sphere, oriented as the boundary of the unit ball $B$. Compute $\int_S\omega$ directly with the parametrisation $\varphi(\theta,\phi)=(\sin\theta\cos\phi,\ \sin\theta\sin\phi,\ \cos\theta)$, $0\le\theta\le\pi$, $0\le\phi\le2\pi$, and compare with $\int_Bd\omega$.
blocks.solution:
Pulling back a $2$-form $A\,dy\wedge dz+B\,dz\wedge dx+C\,dx\wedge dy$ along $\varphi$ gives $(A,B,C)\cdot(\varphi_\theta\times\varphi_\phi)\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$, because each $dx_i\wedge dx_j$ pulls back to a $2\times2$ minor of the Jacobian. Here
$$\varphi_\theta\times\varphi_\phi=\sin\theta\,(\sin\theta\cos\phi,\ \sin\theta\sin\phi,\ \cos\theta)=\sin\theta\,\varphi,$$
which points outward, so the order $(\theta,\phi)$ matches the induced orientation. With $(A,B,C)=\varphi$ the pullback is $\sin\theta\,|\varphi|^2\,d\theta\wedge d\phi=\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$, and
$$\int_S\omega=\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^\pi\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi=4\pi .$$
On the other side, $d\omega=(1+1+1)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$, so $\int_Bd\omega=3\cdot\tfrac43\pi=4\pi$. This is the divergence theorem for the field $(x,y,z)$, whose divergence is $3$.

blocks.title: Closed but not exact
blocks.body:
On the punctured plane $U=\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{0\}$ let
$$\omega=\frac{-y\,dx+x\,dy}{x^2+y^2}.$$
Show that $d\omega=0$ but that $\omega\ne df$ for every smooth function $f$ on $U$. Then show that on the slit plane, $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the closed negative $x$-axis removed, $\omega$ is exact.
blocks.solution:
Write $\omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy$ with $P=-y/(x^2+y^2)$ and $Q=x/(x^2+y^2)$. Then
$$\partial_xQ=\frac{y^2-x^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}=\partial_yP,$$
so $d\omega=(\partial_xQ-\partial_yP)\,dx\wedge dy=0$.

Suppose $\omega=df$ on $U$. For the unit circle $\gamma$, a closed curve, $\int_\gamma df=\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d}{dt}f(\gamma(t))\,dt=f(\gamma(2\pi))-f(\gamma(0))=0$. (This is Stokes for a $1$-dimensional manifold with empty boundary.) But $\gamma^*\omega=dt$ exactly as in the Green's theorem example, because $x^2+y^2=1$ on the circle, so $\int_\gamma\omega=2\pi\ne0$. Contradiction.

On the slit plane every point can be written uniquely as $(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)$ with $-\pi< \theta< \pi$, and $\theta$ is a smooth function there. Differentiating $\tan\theta=y/x$ (or using the polar pullback) gives $d\theta=\omega$. So $\omega$ is exact on the slit plane, and $\int_\gamma\omega=2\pi$ is the total change in angle around the hole. The failure of exactness on $U$ detects the hole; making this precise is the start of de Rham cohomology.

blocks.body:
- Order matters: $dx\wedge dy=-dy\wedge dx$. Reordering a wedge product without tracking signs is the most common source of errors, especially in the induced boundary orientation.
- A $k$-form can only be integrated over a $k$-dimensional oriented object. Integrating $dx\wedge dy$ "along a curve" has no meaning, and without an orientation even $\int_M\omega$ is only defined up to sign.
- Closed does not imply exact. The implication holds on open sets that are star-shaped (Poincaré lemma) but fails on the punctured plane, as shown in the example "Closed but not exact".
- The theorem needs compact support or a compact manifold. Take $M=(0,1)$, which has no boundary points in the manifold sense, and the $0$-form $\omega=x$, which does not have compact support in $M$: then $\int_M d\omega=\int_0^1 dx=1$, not $0$, because the boundary points have been thrown away.
- $d$ of a $1$-form is not a gradient. Under the dictionary it is a curl, and the dictionary between $2$-forms and vector fields uses the Euclidean metric and orientation of $\mathbb{R}^3$, while $d$ itself needs neither.

Forms are the natural integrands on [[smooth-manifolds]], where they are defined chart by chart and the coordinate formula for $d$ turns out not to depend on the chart. On a Riemannian manifold ([[riemannian-geometry]]) the metric adds a volume form and the Hodge star, which converts $k$-forms into $(n-k)$-forms and recovers gradient, curl and divergence on any manifold. The quotient of closed $k$-forms by exact ones is the de Rham cohomology; de Rham's theorem says it agrees with real singular cohomology, linking calculus to [[homology]]. The Gauss–Bonnet theorem ([[gauss-bonnet]]) can be proved by applying Stokes to a connection $1$-form whose derivative is curvature times area. In physics, the electromagnetic field is a $2$-form $F$ on spacetime, and two of Maxwell's equations are simply $dF=0$; the other two say $d{\star}F$ is the current $3$-form, up to constants and sign conventions. In complex analysis, $d(f\,dz)=\partial_{\bar z}f\,d\bar z\wedge dz$, which vanishes for holomorphic $f$; this gives Cauchy's theorem (see [[holomorphic]]).

1. Compute $d\omega$ for $\omega=xy\,dz+yz\,dx+zx\,dy$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$, and check that $d(d\omega)=0$.
2. Show that the pullback of $dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$ under spherical coordinates $$(\rho,\theta,\phi)\mapsto(\rho\sin\theta\cos\phi,\rho\sin\theta\sin\phi,\rho\cos\theta)$$ is $\rho^2\sin\theta\,d\rho\wedge d\theta\wedge d\phi$.
3. Use the Stokes theorem to show that the integral of an exact $2$-form $d\eta$ over the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is $0$, and deduce that the form $\omega/(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}$, with $\omega$ as in the sphere example, is closed but not exact on $\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\{0\}$.
4. Write down $\partial I^2$ explicitly as four oriented edges and check that it is the boundary of the unit square traversed counterclockwise.

checks.python:
import sympy as sp
t,x,y=sp.symbols('t x y')
X,Y=sp.cos(t),sp.sin(t)
I=sp.integrate((-Y)*sp.diff(X,t)+X*sp.diff(Y,t),(t,0,2*sp.pi))
assert sp.simplify(I-2*sp.pi)==0

assert sp.diff(Q,x)-sp.diff(P,y)==2

checks.claim: d∘d=0 in R^3 via the dictionary: curl(grad f)=0 and div(curl F)=0 for arbitrary smooth f, F
checks.python:
import sympy as sp
x,y,z=sp.symbols('x y z')
f=sp.Function('f')(x,y,z)
F=[sp.Function(n)(x,y,z) for n in ('F1','F2','F3')]
def curl(G):
    return [sp.diff(G[2],y)-sp.diff(G[1],z),sp.diff(G[0],z)-sp.diff(G[2],x),sp.diff(G[1],x)-sp.diff(G[0],y)]
def div(G):
    return sp.diff(G[0],x)+sp.diff(G[1],y)+sp.diff(G[2],z)
g=[sp.diff(f,v) for v in (x,y,z)]
assert all(sp.simplify(c)==0 for c in curl(g))
assert sp.simplify(div(curl(F)))==0

entry.sum: A Riemannian metric on a smooth manifold is a smoothly varying inner product $g_p$ on each tangent space; it lets one measure lengths, angles and volumes intrinsically, without an ambient space. Every metric has a unique torsion-free compatible connection, the Levi-Civita connection, whose geodesics are the locally length-minimising curves, and whose failure to commute is the Riemann curvature tensor, which in dimension two reduces to Gaussian curvature.
entry.why: It is the setting of general relativity, where gravity is the curvature of a (Lorentzian) metric, and of most of modern geometry: curvature bounds control topology, as in the Bonnet–Myers and Gauss–Bonnet theorems.

links.note: Curvature restricts topology: by Bonnet–Myers a complete manifold with Ricci curvature bounded below by a positive constant is compact with finite fundamental group, and Gauss–Bonnet turns total curvature of a closed surface into its Euler characteristic.
Gradient descent and Newton methods on curved parameter spaces (matrix manifolds, the natural-gradient method in statistics) move along geodesics or retractions defined by a Riemannian metric.
The metric defines the Laplace–Beltrami operator, and the heat and wave equations on a manifold, whose spectrum encodes geometric data such as volume and total curvature.

refs: Lee, Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds
do Carmo, Riemannian Geometry
Petersen, Riemannian Geometry

blocks.body:
On a surface in $\mathbb{R}^3$, lengths of curves are computed with the first fundamental form, and Gauss discovered that the curvature of the surface can be computed from that form alone (see [[surfaces-curvature]]). An ant living on the surface, measuring only distances, could detect that it lives on a sphere rather than a plane. Riemann's idea was to take this seriously: forget the surrounding space and simply declare, on any smooth manifold, how to measure the length of tangent vectors.

This page builds the three basic tools of that programme: the metric itself, the geodesics (the straightest possible curves), and curvature (the obstruction to the space being flat). The examples are the three model geometries, flat space, the round sphere and the hyperbolic plane, which every later theorem is compared with.

blocks.title: Riemannian metric
blocks.body:
A Riemannian metric $g$ on a smooth manifold $M$ is a choice, for each $p\in M$, of an inner product $g_p=\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_p$ on the tangent space $T_pM$, depending smoothly on $p$: in any chart with coordinates $x^1,\dots,x^n$ the functions $g_{ij}=\langle\partial_i,\partial_j\rangle$ are smooth. Then $(g_{ij})$ is a symmetric positive definite matrix at each point, and one writes $g=g_{ij}\,dx^i\,dx^j$ (summation over repeated indices). As an element of [[tensor-products|the tensor algebra]], $g$ is a smooth symmetric positive definite section of $T^*M\otimes T^*M$.

The length of a piecewise smooth curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ is $L(\gamma)=\int_a^b\sqrt{g(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)}\,dt$, and the distance $d(p,q)$ is the infimum of lengths of curves from $p$ to $q$. Meaning: the metric is an infinitesimal ruler and protractor attached to every point.

blocks.title: Three model geometries
blocks.body:
1. Euclidean space: $g=dx_1^2+\cdots+dx_n^2$, so $g_{ij}=\delta_{ij}$.
2. The round sphere $S^2$, in coordinates $(\theta,\phi)$ (polar angle and longitude): $g=d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2$. This is the metric induced from $\mathbb{R}^3$.
3. The hyperbolic upper half-plane $H=\{(x,y):y>0\}$: $g=\dfrac{dx^2+dy^2}{y^2}$. Angles are the Euclidean angles, but lengths are stretched by $1/y$, so the $x$-axis is infinitely far away.

A quick computation in $H$: the vertical segment from $(0,a)$ to $(0,b)$, $0< a< b$, has length $\int_a^b dy/y=\ln(b/a)$. Going from height $1$ to height $e^{-10}$ costs only $10$ units, yet any path down to the axis has infinite length. The horizontal segment from $(0,1)$ to $(1,1)$ has length $1$, but it is not the shortest path: the arc of the circle through these points centred on the $x$-axis, at $(\tfrac12,0)$, has length $\ln\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}\approx0.962$. Climbing to where lengths are cheaper and coming back down pays off.

Every smooth manifold carries some Riemannian metric: in each chart take the Euclidean one and glue with a partition of unity, using the fact that a positive combination of inner products is an inner product. So the question is never whether a metric exists but which metrics are interesting.

blocks.title: Why a connection is needed
blocks.body:
To say that a curve is straight we want its acceleration to be zero. In $\mathbb{R}^n$ the acceleration is the derivative of the velocity vector, which compares vectors at nearby points by translating one to the other. On a manifold, $T_pM$ and $T_qM$ are different vector spaces and there is no canonical way to compare them. The fix is an extra structure, an affine connection: an operator $
abla$ taking vector fields $X,Y$ to a vector field $
abla_XY$, which is $C^\infty(M)$-linear in $X$, $\mathbb{R}$-linear in $Y$, and satisfies the Leibniz rule $
abla_X(fY)=(Xf)\,Y+f\,
abla_XY$. In coordinates a connection is determined by $n^3$ functions, the Christoffel symbols, defined by $
abla_{\partial_i}\partial_j=\Gamma^k_{ij}\partial_k$.

On a surface in $\mathbb{R}^3$ the obvious choice is to differentiate $Y$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and project back onto the tangent plane. Two properties of that choice determine it completely and make sense on any Riemannian manifold; they are the content of the next theorem.

blocks.title: Fundamental theorem of Riemannian geometry
blocks.body:
On a Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ there is exactly one affine connection $\nabla$ that is

1. torsion-free: $\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX=[X,Y]$ for all vector fields $X,Y$, and
2. compatible with $g$: $X\langle Y,Z\rangle=\langle\nabla_XY,Z\rangle+\langle Y,\nabla_XZ\rangle$ for all $X,Y,Z$.

It is called the Levi-Civita connection, and its Christoffel symbols are
$$\Gamma^k_{ij}=\tfrac12\,g^{kl}\big(\partial_ig_{jl}+\partial_jg_{il}-\partial_lg_{ij}\big),$$
where $(g^{kl})$ is the inverse matrix of $(g_{ij})$.

Uniqueness. Suppose $
abla$ has both properties. Write compatibility three times with the letters cycled:
$$X\langle Y,Zangle=\langle
abla_XY,Zangle+\langle Y,
abla_XZangle,\quad Y\langle Z,Xangle=\langle
abla_YZ,Xangle+\langle Z,
abla_YXangle,\quad Z\langle X,Yangle=\langle
abla_ZX,Yangle+\langle X,
abla_ZYangle .$$
Add the first two and subtract the third. Grouping terms and using torsion-freeness in the forms $
abla_XZ-
abla_ZX=[X,Z]$, $
abla_YZ-
abla_ZY=[Y,Z]$ and $
abla_YX=
abla_XY-[X,Y]$, we get the Koszul formula
$$2\langle
abla_XY,Zangle=X\langle Y,Zangle+Y\langle Z,Xangle-Z\langle X,Yangle+\langle[X,Y],Zangle-\langle[X,Z],Yangle-\langle[Y,Z],Xangle .$$
The right side does not mention $
abla$, and since $g$ is non-degenerate, knowing $\langle
abla_XY,Zangle$ for all $Z$ determines $
abla_XY$. So there is at most one such connection.

The formula for $\Gamma$. Take $X=\partial_i$, $Y=\partial_j$, $Z=\partial_l$; coordinate fields have zero brackets, so $2\,\Gamma^k_{ij}g_{kl}=\partial_ig_{jl}+\partial_jg_{il}-\partial_lg_{ij}$. Multiplying by $g^{lm}$ and summing over $l$ gives the stated formula.

Existence. In each chart define $
abla$ by $
abla_{\partial_i}\partial_j=\Gamma^k_{ij}\partial_k$ with $\Gamma$ given by the formula, extended by the linearity and Leibniz rules. Then $\Gamma^k_{ij}=\Gamma^k_{ji}$, which is torsion-freeness in coordinates, and a direct computation gives $\partial_ig_{jl}=\Gamma^k_{ij}g_{kl}+\Gamma^k_{il}g_{jk}$, which is compatibility in coordinates. On the overlap of two charts both definitions have the two properties, so by uniqueness they agree, and the local definitions patch together.

blocks.title: Geodesic
blocks.body:
A smooth curve $\gamma$ is a geodesic if its acceleration $D_t\dot\gamma=\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma$ vanishes. In coordinates $\gamma(t)=(\gamma^1(t),\dots,\gamma^n(t))$ this is the system of second-order ODEs
$$\ddot\gamma^k+\Gamma^k_{ij}(\gamma)\,\dot\gamma^i\dot\gamma^j=0,\qquad k=1,\dots,n .$$
By ODE existence and uniqueness, for each $p\in M$ and $v\in T_pM$ there is a unique maximal geodesic with $\gamma(0)=p$, $\dot\gamma(0)=v$. Compatibility implies $\frac{d}{dt}\langle\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma\rangle=2\langle D_t\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma\rangle=0$, so geodesics have constant speed.

Meaning: geodesics are curves that do not turn, as seen from inside the manifold. They are exactly the constant-speed critical points of the energy $\tfrac12\int g(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)\,dt$; the geodesic equation is its Euler–Lagrange equation (see [[calculus-of-variations]]).

blocks.title: Geodesics minimise, but only locally
blocks.body:
Two standard facts, stated here without proof (both are in the references):

1. Every point $p$ has a neighbourhood $U$ such that for $q\in U$ the radial geodesic from $p$ to $q$ inside $U$ is, up to reparametrisation, the unique shortest curve between them. So every curve of minimal length, parametrised at constant speed, is a geodesic.
2. Hopf–Rinow theorem: for a connected Riemannian manifold the following are equivalent: $M$ is complete as a metric space; every geodesic is defined for all time; closed and bounded subsets are compact. When they hold, any two points are joined by a minimising geodesic.

The converse of the first fact fails globally. On the unit sphere the great circles are the geodesics, and a great-circle arc longer than $\pi$ is a geodesic but not the shortest path between its endpoints; the other arc of the same great circle is shorter.

In physics, a free particle moves along a geodesic, since its Lagrangian is the kinetic energy $\tfrac12 g(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)$; in general relativity, with a metric of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, freely falling bodies follow timelike geodesics.

blocks.title: Riemann curvature and sectional curvature
blocks.body:
The Riemann curvature endomorphism of the Levi-Civita connection is
$$R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z .$$
It is $C^\infty(M)$-linear in each argument, hence a tensor: its value at $p$ depends only on $X_p,Y_p,Z_p$. In coordinates $R(\partial_i,\partial_j)\partial_k=R^l{}_{ijk}\,\partial_l$ with
$$R^l{}_{ijk}=\partial_i\Gamma^l_{jk}-\partial_j\Gamma^l_{ik}+\Gamma^l_{im}\Gamma^m_{jk}-\Gamma^l_{jm}\Gamma^m_{ik}.$$
For a 2-dimensional subspace $\sigma\subseteq T_pM$ spanned by $X,Y$ the sectional curvature is
$$K(\sigma)=\frac{\langle R(X,Y)Y,X\rangle}{|X|^2|Y|^2-\langle X,Y\rangle^2},$$
which does not depend on the chosen basis of $\sigma$. The Ricci curvature is the trace $\operatorname{Ric}(Y,Z)=\operatorname{tr}(X\mapsto R(X,Y)Z)$ and the scalar curvature is the trace of Ricci with respect to $g$.

Meaning: $R$ measures how much transporting a vector around a tiny loop rotates it. On a surface $K$ equals the Gaussian curvature, which is Gauss's Theorema Egregium seen from the intrinsic side. Flat space has $R=0$, the unit sphere has $K\equiv1$, the hyperbolic plane has $K\equiv-1$.

blocks.title: Curvature of a rotationally symmetric surface metric
blocks.body:
Let $g=dr^2+f(r)^2\,d\theta^2$ on a region where $f>0$. Then its Gaussian (sectional) curvature is
$$K=-\frac{f''(r)}{f(r)} .$$

With coordinates $(x^1,x^2)=(r,\theta)$ we have $g_{11}=1$, $g_{12}=0$, $g_{22}=f^2$. The Christoffel formula gives the only nonzero symbols
$$\Gamma^1_{22}=-ff',\qquad \Gamma^2_{12}=\Gamma^2_{21}=\frac{f'}{f}.$$
Now compute $R(\partial_r,\partial_\theta)\partial_\theta$. Its $\partial_r$-component is
$$R^1{}_{122}=\partial_r\Gamma^1_{22}-\partial_\theta\Gamma^1_{12}+\Gamma^1_{1m}\Gamma^m_{22}-\Gamma^1_{2m}\Gamma^m_{12}=-(f'^2+ff'')-0+0-\Gamma^1_{22}\Gamma^2_{12}=-f'^2-ff''+f'^2=-ff''.$$
So $\langle R(\partial_r,\partial_\theta)\partial_\theta,\partial_r\rangle=g_{11}R^1{}_{122}=-ff''$. The denominator is $|\partial_r|^2|\partial_\theta|^2-0=f^2$, so $K=-ff''/f^2=-f''/f$.

blocks.title: The round sphere
blocks.body: For $g=d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2$ on the sphere minus the poles, find the Christoffel symbols and the curvature. Show that the equator is a geodesic and that no other circle of latitude is.
blocks.solution:
This is the theorem's metric with $r=\theta$ and $f=\sin\theta$, so the nonzero symbols are $\Gamma^\theta_{\phi\phi}=-\sin\theta\cos\theta$ and $\Gamma^\phi_{\theta\phi}=\Gamma^\phi_{\phi\theta}=\cot\theta$, and $K=-(-\sin\theta)/\sin\theta=1$.

The geodesic equations are
$$\ddot\theta-\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\dot\phi^2=0,\qquad \ddot\phi+2\cot\theta\,\dot\theta\dot\phi=0 .$$
For a latitude circle $\theta\equiv\theta_0$, $\phi=t$, the second equation holds and the first reduces to $\sin\theta_0\cos\theta_0=0$. With $0< \theta_0< \pi$ this forces $\theta_0=\pi/2$: the equator is a geodesic and the others are not. Meridians $\phi\equiv\phi_0$, $\theta=t$ satisfy both equations, and rotating the sphere shows that all great circles are geodesics.

A latitude circle near the north pole visibly bends towards the pole; that bending is the nonzero term $\sin\theta_0\cos\theta_0\,\dot\phi^2$.

blocks.title: The hyperbolic plane
blocks.body: For $g=(dx^2+dy^2)/y^2$ on $y>0$ compute the Christoffel symbols and the curvature. Check that vertical lines and the unit-speed curves $x=c+\rho\tanh t$, $y=\rho\operatorname{sech}t$ (with $c\in\mathbb{R}$, $\rho>0$) are geodesics, and identify the second family geometrically.
blocks.solution:
Here $g_{11}=g_{22}=y^{-2}$ and $g^{11}=g^{22}=y^2$. Only $\partial_y$ derivatives are nonzero, $\partial_yg_{11}=\partial_yg_{22}=-2y^{-3}$, and the formula gives
$$\Gamma^x_{xy}=\Gamma^x_{yx}=-\frac1y,\qquad \Gamma^y_{xx}=\frac1y,\qquad \Gamma^y_{yy}=-\frac1y,$$
all others zero. The geodesic equations are
$$\ddot x-\frac2y\,\dot x\dot y=0,\qquad \ddot y+\frac1y\,\dot x^2-\frac1y\,\dot y^2=0 .$$
A vertical line $x=c$, $y=e^t$ satisfies both: the first trivially, the second because $\ddot y=e^t=\dot y^2/y$. Its speed is $|\dot y|/y=1$.

For $x=c+\rho\tanh t$, $y=\rho\operatorname{sech}t$ we have $(x-c)^2+y^2=\rho^2(\tanh^2t+\operatorname{sech}^2t)=\rho^2$, so this curve runs along the upper semicircle of radius $\rho$ centred at $(c,0)$. Differentiating, $\dot x=\rho\operatorname{sech}^2t$ and $\dot y=-\rho\operatorname{sech}t\tanh t$, so $(\dot x^2+\dot y^2)/y^2=\operatorname{sech}^2t+\tanh^2t=1$, and substituting into the two equations gives zero (checked symbolically in the checks below). So the geodesics are the vertical lines and the semicircles meeting the boundary at right angles.

For the curvature, the inverse matrix is diagonal, and the coordinate formula for $R^l{}_{ijk}$ gives $\langle R(\partial_x,\partial_y)\partial_y,\partial_x\rangle=-y^{-4}$. Dividing by $|\partial_x|^2|\partial_y|^2=y^{-4}$ gives $K\equiv-1$. Alternatively, in geodesic polar coordinates about any point the metric is $dr^2+\sinh^2r\,d\theta^2$, and the theorem gives $K=-\sinh r/\sinh r=-1$. Through a point off a geodesic there are infinitely many geodesics that never meet it, so Euclid's parallel postulate fails.

blocks.title: Detecting curvature with a piece of string
blocks.body:
Suppose that around a point $p$ of a surface the metric in geodesic polar coordinates is rotationally symmetric, $dr^2+f(r)^2\,d\theta^2$ with $f(0)=0$ and $f'(0)=1$ (as for a surface of revolution with $p$ on the axis). The geodesic circle of radius $r$ about $p$ has circumference $C(r)=2\pi f(r)$. Show that
$$K(p)=\lim_{r\to0}\frac{3\,(2\pi r-C(r))}{\pi r^3},$$
assuming $f$ is smooth with $f''(0)=0$, and check the formula on the unit sphere.
blocks.solution:
By the theorem, $f''=-Kf$, with $K$ evaluated along the radial geodesic. Differentiating, $f'''=-K'f-Kf'$, so at $r=0$ we get $f'''(0)=-K(p)$. Taylor's theorem then gives
$$f(r)=r-\frac{K(p)}{6}\,r^3+O(r^4),\qquad C(r)=2\pi r-\frac{\pi K(p)}{3}\,r^3+O(r^4).$$
So $2\pi r-C(r)=\frac{\pi K(p)}{3}r^3+O(r^4)$, and multiplying by $3/(\pi r^3)$ and letting $r\to0$ gives $K(p)$.

On the unit sphere $f=\sin r$, so $C(r)=2\pi\sin r=2\pi r-\frac{\pi}{3}r^3+\cdots$ and the limit is $1$. In words: a surveyor on a positively curved surface who pegs out a circle of radius $r$ finds the circumference shorter than $2\pi r$, and the deficit measures the curvature. On the hyperbolic plane, $f=\sinh r$ and the circumference is longer. Without rotational symmetry the same limit still holds, with $C(r)$ the length of the geodesic circle (the Bertrand–Diguet–Puiseux theorem, stated here without proof).

blocks.title: Curvature and global shape
blocks.body:
Curvature is local, but lower and upper bounds on it have global consequences. Two theorems, stated without proof:

1. Bonnet–Myers: if $M^n$, $n\ge2$, is complete and $\operatorname{Ric}\ge(n-1)k\,g$ for some $k>0$, then $M$ has diameter at most $\pi/\sqrt k$, so $M$ is compact and its fundamental group is finite. The bound is attained by the round sphere of radius $1/\sqrt k$.
2. Cartan–Hadamard: if $M^n$ is complete, simply connected and has all sectional curvatures $\le0$, then the exponential map at any point is a diffeomorphism $\mathbb{R}^n\to M$.

In dimension two, the Gauss–Bonnet theorem ties total curvature to topology: $\int_MK\,dA=2\pi\chi(M)$ for a closed surface (see [[gauss-bonnet]]). In general relativity the Einstein field equations set a combination of Ricci and scalar curvature equal to the energy–momentum tensor.

- Sign and index conventions differ between books. Some define $R(X,Y)$ with the opposite sign or order the indices of $R^l{}_{ijk}$ differently. The sanity check is always the same: with your conventions the unit sphere must come out with $K=+1$.
- Christoffel symbols are not the components of a tensor. They can be nonzero in flat space (polar coordinates in the plane have $\Gamma^r_{\theta\theta}=-r$) and can be made zero at any one point by a choice of coordinates. Curvature cannot be removed by a coordinate change.
- A geodesic need not be the shortest curve between its endpoints, and two points can be joined by many geodesics (antipodal points of a sphere are joined by infinitely many).
- Being geodesically incomplete is not the same as being non-compact: $\mathbb{R}^n$ is non-compact and complete; an open ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is incomplete.
- In dimension three and up, Gaussian curvature is replaced by sectional curvature, which depends on a choice of plane; Ricci and scalar curvature are averages of it and carry less information.

The page builds on [[smooth-manifolds]] for tangent spaces and vector fields, on [[tensor-products]] for the metric and curvature tensors, and on [[surfaces-curvature]] for the two-dimensional picture. The metric gives a volume form, which makes integration of functions possible and, via the Hodge star, the Laplace–Beltrami operator on [[differential-forms]]. Gauss–Bonnet ([[gauss-bonnet]]) is the global theorem for surfaces. Bi-invariant metrics on compact [[lie-groups]] have the one-parameter subgroups as their geodesics through the identity, and they have non-negative sectional curvature. Geodesics as critical points of energy are a central example in the [[calculus-of-variations]], and the hyperbolic plane connects to complex analysis through its isometry group of Möbius transformations (see [[conformal-maps]]).

1. Show that the metric $g=dr^2+r^2d\theta^2$ on the punctured plane has curvature $0$, and compute its Christoffel symbols.
2. In the upper half-plane, use the geodesic equations to show that a geodesic with $\dot x(0)\ne0$ satisfies $\dot x/y^2=\text{constant}$, and deduce that it is not a vertical line.
3. Verify that the hyperbolic distance from $(0,1)$ to $(1,1)$ is $\ln\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}$ by integrating along the semicircle centred at $(\tfrac12,0)$.
4. For the metric $dr^2+f(r)^2d\theta^2$, find all $f$ with $f(0)=0$, $f'(0)=1$ for which the curvature is a constant $K$, treating $K>0$, $K=0$ and $K<0$ separately.

entry.sum: A norm $\|\cdot\|$ on a real or complex vector space measures the size of vectors, subject to positivity, homogeneity and the triangle inequality; it makes the space a metric space with $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$. A Banach space is a normed space that is complete, so that Cauchy sequences, and absolutely convergent series, converge. In finite dimensions all norms are equivalent and every normed space is complete; in infinite dimensions the choice of norm matters, and linear maps are continuous exactly when they are bounded.
entry.why: Most of analysis happens in spaces of functions, and a norm is what makes "close to", "converges" and "approximately" meaningful there; completeness is what lets existence proofs (fixed points, series solutions, limits of approximations) produce an actual object.

links.note: Error estimates and condition numbers are stated in operator norms, such as $\kappa(A)=\|A\|\,\|A^{-1}\|$, which bounds how relative errors in data are amplified when solving $Ax=b$.
The Picard–Lindelöf existence theorem applies the contraction mapping principle in the Banach space $C[a,b]$ with the sup norm.
Weak solutions of partial differential equations are found in Banach spaces of functions such as Sobolev spaces, where completeness lets approximate solutions converge to a genuine one.

refs: Kreyszig, Introductory Functional Analysis with Applications
Folland, Real Analysis: Modern Techniques and Their Applications
Brezis, Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and Partial Differential Equations

blocks.body:
How far apart are the functions $\sin x$ and $x$ on $[0,1]$? One answer is the largest gap between their graphs; another is the area between them. Both are reasonable, they give different numbers, and they lead to different notions of convergence. A norm is a precise rule of this kind for measuring the size of a vector, and therefore, through $\|f-g\|$, the distance between two vectors.

Normed spaces combine the two prerequisites of this page: they are [[vector-spaces]], so we can add and scale, and they are [[metric-spaces]], so we can take limits. The central extra condition is completeness, which separates spaces where limits can be trusted to exist (Banach spaces) from spaces with holes.

blocks.title: Norm
Examples, and the shapes of unit balls
blocks.body:
On $\mathbb{R}^n$ there are many norms. For $1\le p< \infty$ put $\|x\|_p=(|x_1|^p+\cdots+|x_n|^p)^{1/p}$, and put $\|x\|_\infty=\max_i|x_i|$. For $x=(3,-4)$ we get $\|x\|_1=7$, $\|x\|_2=5$ and $\|x\|_\infty=4$. The triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_p$ is Minkowski's inequality; for $p=2$ it follows from [[cauchy-schwarz]].

The unit ball $\{x:\|x\|\le1\}$ shows the geometry. In $\mathbb{R}^2$ the $1$-ball is a diamond, the $2$-ball a disc, the $\infty$-ball a square, and the $p$-balls interpolate between them. Every unit ball of a norm is convex, symmetric about $0$, and absorbs every direction; conversely, in $\mathbb{R}^n$ any bounded closed convex set symmetric about $0$ with $0$ in its interior is the unit ball of exactly one norm. For $p<1$ the formula still makes sense but the ball is not convex, and the triangle inequality fails: with $p=\tfrac12$, $\|(1,0)\|=\|(0,1)\|=1$ but $\|(1,1)\|=(1+1)^2=4$.

The infinite-dimensional analogues are sequence and function spaces:

- $\ell^p$ for $1\le p< \infty$: sequences with $\sum|x_n|^p< \infty$, normed by $(\sum|x_n|^p)^{1/p}$.
- $\ell^\infty$: bounded sequences with $\|x\|_\infty=\sup_n|x_n|$, and its subspace $c_0$ of sequences tending to $0$.
- $C[a,b]$: continuous functions with the sup norm $\|f\|_\infty=\max_{[a,b]}|f|$, or with the integral norm $\|f\|_1=\int_a^b|f|$.

For the opening question, $x-\sin x$ is increasing on $[0,1]$, so $\|x-\sin x\|_\infty=1-\sin1\approx0.159$, while $$\|x-\sin x\|_1=\int_0^1(x-\sin x)\,dx=\cos1-\tfrac12\approx0.040$$.

blocks.title: Banach space
blocks.body:
A sequence $(x_n)$ in a normed space is Cauchy if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N$ with $\|x_n-x_m\|< \varepsilon$ for all $n,m\ge N$. A normed space is a Banach space if every Cauchy sequence converges to a point of the space, that is, if it is complete as a metric space.

Meaning: in a Banach space, a sequence whose terms eventually stop moving really does arrive somewhere.

blocks.title: C[a,b] with the sup norm is a Banach space
blocks.body: The space $C[a,b]$ of continuous real (or complex) functions on $[a,b]$, with $\|f\|_\infty=\max_{x\in[a,b]}|f(x)|$, is complete.

Let $(f_n)$ be Cauchy. For each fixed $x$, $|f_n(x)-f_m(x)|\le\|f_n-f_m\|_\infty$, so $(f_n(x))$ is a Cauchy sequence of numbers and converges; call the limit $f(x)$.

Given $\varepsilon>0$ choose $N$ with $\|f_n-f_m\|_\infty< \varepsilon$ for $n,m\ge N$. Then for every $x$ and every $n,m\ge N$, $|f_n(x)-f_m(x)|< \varepsilon$; letting $m\to\infty$ gives $|f_n(x)-f(x)|\le\varepsilon$ for all $x$ and all $n\ge N$. So $f_n\to f$ uniformly.

A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous (see [[uniform-convergence]]): given $x_0$ and $\varepsilon$, fix $n\ge N$ and use $$|f(x)-f(x_0)|\le|f(x)-f_n(x)|+|f_n(x)-f_n(x_0)|+|f_n(x_0)-f(x_0)|\le2\varepsilon+|f_n(x)-f_n(x_0)|$$, which is less than $3\varepsilon$ for $x$ near $x_0$. Hence $f\in C[a,b]$ and $\|f_n-f\|_\infty\to0$.

blocks.title: The same space, an incomplete norm
blocks.body: In $C[0,1]$ with $\|f\|_1=\int_0^1|f|$, let $f_n$ be $0$ on $[0,\tfrac12]$, rise linearly to $1$ on $[\tfrac12,\tfrac12+\tfrac1n]$, and equal $1$ afterwards ($n\ge2$). Show that $(f_n)$ is Cauchy but has no limit in $C[0,1]$.
blocks.solution:
For $m>n$ we have $f_m\ge f_n$ everywhere, and they differ only on $[\tfrac12,\tfrac12+\tfrac1n]$. Since $\int_0^1f_n=\tfrac12-\tfrac1{2n}$ (a triangle of area $\tfrac1{2n}$ is missing from the full step),
$$\|f_m-f_n\|_1=\int_0^1(f_m-f_n)=\frac1{2n}-\frac1{2m}< \frac1{2n},$$
so the sequence is Cauchy.

Suppose $\|f_n-f\|_1\to0$ for some continuous $f$. On $[0,\tfrac12]$ every $f_n$ is $0$, so $\int_0^{1/2}|f|\le\|f-f_n\|_1\to0$ and $f=0$ there by continuity. For any $\delta>0$, on $[\tfrac12+\delta,1]$ we have $f_n=1$ once $1/n< \delta$, so likewise $f=1$ there. Letting $\delta\to0$, $f$ is $0$ on $[0,\tfrac12]$ and $1$ on $(\tfrac12,1]$, which is not continuous. So $(C[0,1],\|\cdot\|_1)$ is not complete. Its completion is the space $L^1[0,1]$ of [[lp-spaces]], where the step function does live.

blocks.title: Completeness through series
blocks.body: A normed space $X$ is a Banach space if and only if every absolutely convergent series converges: whenever $\sum_n\|x_n\|< \infty$, the partial sums $\sum_{n\le N}x_n$ converge in $X$.

If $X$ is complete and $\sum\|x_n\|< \infty$, the partial sums $s_N$ satisfy $\|s_M-s_N\|\le\sum_{N< n\le M}\|x_n\|$ for $M>N$, which is small for large $N$; so $(s_N)$ is Cauchy and converges.

Conversely, let $(y_k)$ be Cauchy. Choose $k_1< k_2< \cdots$ with $\|y_{k}-y_{l}\|<2^{-j}$ for $k,l\ge k_j$. The series $y_{k_1}+\sum_j(y_{k_{j+1}}-y_{k_j})$ has terms of norm less than $2^{-j}$, so it converges by hypothesis; its partial sums are exactly $y_{k_{j}}$, so this subsequence converges to some $y$. A Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges to the same limit, so $y_k\to y$.

blocks.title: Bounded linear operators
blocks.body:
For linear maps between normed spaces, continuity has a simple test. A linear $T:X\to Y$ is bounded if there is $C$ with $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for all $x$; the smallest such $C$ is the operator norm $\|T\|=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}\|Tx\|$.

Claim: $T$ is continuous if and only if it is bounded. If $T$ is bounded, $\|Tx-Tx'\|\le C\|x-x'\|$, so $T$ is even Lipschitz. If $T$ is continuous at $0$, there is $\delta>0$ with $\|Tx\|\le1$ whenever $\|x\|\le\delta$; for $x\ne0$ apply this to $\delta x/\|x\|$ to get $\|Tx\|\le\|x\|/\delta$.

The bounded operators $X\to Y$ form a normed space $B(X,Y)$ with $\|ST\|\le\|S\|\,\|T\|$, and it is a Banach space whenever $Y$ is (same argument as for $C[a,b]$, applied pointwise on the unit ball). Taking $Y=\mathbb{K}$ gives the dual space $X^*$ of bounded linear functionals, which is always complete; see [[dual-spaces]] and [[hahn-banach]].

In infinite dimensions linear maps need not be bounded. On polynomials on $[0,1]$ with the sup norm, the derivative $D$ has $\|x^n\|_\infty=1$ but $\|Dx^n\|_\infty=n$, so no constant $C$ works and $D$ is discontinuous: the polynomials $x^n/\sqrt n$ tend to $0$, while their derivatives $\sqrt n\,x^{n-1}$ have sup norm $\sqrt n\to\infty$.

blocks.title: Norms on a finite-dimensional space are equivalent
blocks.body: If $X$ is finite-dimensional, any two norms $\|\cdot\|$ and $\|\cdot\|'$ on $X$ are equivalent: there are constants $0< c\le C$ with $c\|x\|\le\|x\|'\le C\|x\|$ for all $x$. Consequently every finite-dimensional normed space is complete, every finite-dimensional subspace of a normed space is closed, and every linear map from a finite-dimensional normed space is bounded.

Choose a basis and identify $X$ with $\mathbb{K}^n$; it is enough to compare an arbitrary norm $\|\cdot\|$ with $\|\cdot\|_1$, since equivalence is transitive. With $e_i$ the basis vectors and $M=\max_i\|e_i\|$, the triangle inequality gives $\|x\|\le\sum|x_i|\,\|e_i\|\le M\|x\|_1$. In particular $\big|\|x\|-\|y\|\big|\le\|x-y\|\le M\|x-y\|_1$, so $\|\cdot\|$ is continuous with respect to $\|\cdot\|_1$.

The unit sphere $S=\{x:\|x\|_1=1\}$ is closed and bounded in $\mathbb{K}^n$, hence compact (see [[compactness]]). The continuous function $\|\cdot\|$ attains a minimum $m$ on $S$, and $m>0$ because $0\notin S$. For $x\ne0$, $x/\|x\|_1\in S$, so $\|x\|\ge m\|x\|_1$. Thus $m\|x\|_1\le\|x\|\le M\|x\|_1$.

For the consequences: $\mathbb{K}^n$ is complete in $\|\cdot\|_1$, and equivalent norms have the same Cauchy sequences and limits. A finite-dimensional subspace is complete, hence closed. For linear $T$ on $\mathbb{K}^n$, $\|Tx\|\le\sum|x_i|\,\|Te_i\|\le(\max_i\|Te_i\|)\,\|x\|_1$, which is bounded by a constant times the given norm.

blocks.title: What changes in infinite dimensions
blocks.body:
The proof above used compactness of the unit sphere, and that is exactly what infinite-dimensional spaces lack. In $\ell^p$ the unit vectors $e_n$ (a $1$ in position $n$) satisfy $\|e_n-e_m\|_p=2^{1/p}$ for $n\ne m$, so no subsequence is Cauchy and the closed unit ball is not compact, although it is closed and bounded. Riesz's lemma shows this always happens: the closed unit ball of a normed space is compact if and only if the space is finite-dimensional.

Two other consequences recur throughout functional analysis. First, on an infinite-dimensional space there are always inequivalent norms, as $\|\cdot\|_1$ and $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ on $C[0,1]$ show. Second, which norm one picks decides which sequences converge and which maps are continuous, so in applications the norm is chosen to fit the problem: the sup norm for uniform approximation, $L^2$ norms for energy, Sobolev norms for PDE.

blocks.title: Operator norms of a matrix
blocks.body: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$. Compute its operator norm on $\mathbb{R}^2$ with $\|\cdot\|_\infty$, with $\|\cdot\|_1$ and with $\|\cdot\|_2$.
blocks.solution:
With $\|\cdot\|_\infty$: for $\|x\|_\infty\le1$, $|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_j|a_{ij}|$, and equality is reached by taking $x_j=\pm1$ with the signs of row $i$. So $\|A\|_\infty$ is the largest absolute row sum, $\max(1+2,\,0+3)=3$.

With $\|\cdot\|_1$: $\|Ax\|_1\le\sum_j|x_j|\sum_i|a_{ij}|$, and equality is reached at a standard basis vector. So $\|A\|_1$ is the largest absolute column sum, $\max(1,\,5)=5$.

With $\|\cdot\|_2$: $\|Ax\|_2^2=x^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}Ax$, which on the unit circle is maximised at the largest eigenvalue of $A^{\mathsf T}A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&13\end{pmatrix}$ (see [[spectral-theorem]]). Its eigenvalues are $7\pm2\sqrt{10}$, and $7+2\sqrt{10}=(\sqrt5+\sqrt2)^2$, so $\|A\|_2=\sqrt5+\sqrt2\approx3.65$, the largest singular value. Three norms, three answers, as the equivalence theorem allows.

blocks.title: Which ℓ^p norms come from an inner product?
blocks.body: A norm comes from an inner product only if it satisfies the parallelogram law $\|x+y\|^2+\|x-y\|^2=2\|x\|^2+2\|y\|^2$. Show that on $\mathbb{R}^2$ the norm $\|\cdot\|_p$ ($1\le p\le\infty$) satisfies this law only for $p=2$.
blocks.solution:
Test with $x=e_1=(1,0)$ and $y=e_2=(0,1)$. The right side is $2+2=4$. For $p< \infty$, $\|e_1\pm e_2\|_p=2^{1/p}$, so the left side is $2\cdot2^{2/p}$. Equality requires $2^{2/p}=2$, that is $p=2$. For $p=\infty$, $\|e_1\pm e_2\|_\infty=1$ and the left side is $2\ne4$.

For $p=2$ the law holds because $\|x\|_2^2=x\cdot x$ and expanding gives $\|x+y\|^2+\|x-y\|^2=2x\cdot x+2y\cdot y$. Normed spaces whose norm comes from a complete inner product are the [[hilbert-spaces]], the best-behaved Banach spaces.

blocks.body:
- Completeness belongs to the norm, not to the vector space: $C[0,1]$ is complete with $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ and incomplete with $\|\cdot\|_1$.
- In infinite dimensions, closed and bounded does not imply compact, and linear does not imply continuous. Both are true in finite dimensions only.
- A subspace of a Banach space is a Banach space only if it is closed. The polynomials form a non-closed subspace of $C[0,1]$; by the Weierstrass theorem their closure is all of $C[0,1]$.
- The formula $(\sum|x_i|^p)^{1/p}$ is not a norm for $0< p<1$.
- The operator norm depends on the norms chosen on both sides; "the norm of a matrix" is ambiguous until those are fixed.

Banach spaces are the stage for most of functional analysis. The [[lp-spaces]] with $1\le p< \infty$ are the completions of continuous functions under integral norms ($L^\infty$ is not: continuous functions are not dense in it). [[hilbert-spaces]] add an inner product and with it orthogonality and projections. The [[hahn-banach]] theorem guarantees that the dual space of a normed space is large enough to separate points. The contraction mapping principle ([[contraction-mapping]]) needs only a complete metric, and its most common setting is a closed subset of a Banach space, which is how existence theorems for ODEs are proved. The theory of [[compact-operators]] studies the operators that behave most like matrices, and [[fourier-series]] provide the classic examples of convergence that holds in one norm and fails in another.

entry.sum: A Hilbert space is a vector space with an inner product $\langle x,y\rangle$ that is complete for the norm $\|x\|=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$, such as $\mathbb{C}^n$, the sequence space $\ell^2$ or the function space $L^2$. Completeness plus the parallelogram law give nearest points in closed convex sets and orthogonal projections onto closed subspaces; from these follow the Riesz representation theorem and expansions $x=\sum\langle x,e_n\rangle e_n$ in an orthonormal basis, with Parseval's identity.
key: H=M\oplus M^{\perp}\quad\text{for every closed subspace } M
entry.why: Hilbert spaces carry Euclidean geometry (angles, orthogonality, best approximation) into infinite dimensions; they are the setting of Fourier series, least-squares approximation, quantum mechanics, and the weak formulation of partial differential equations.

links.note: Weak solutions of elliptic equations such as $-\Delta u=f$ with $u=0$ on the boundary are obtained from the Riesz representation theorem (or the Lax–Milgram theorem) in the Sobolev Hilbert space $H^1_0$.

Fourier series are expansions in the orthonormal basis $e^{inx}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ of $L^2[-\pi,\pi]$, and Parseval's identity says that $f\mapsto(\langle f,e_n\rangle)_n$ is an isometry of $L^2[-\pi,\pi]$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$; its analogue for the Fourier transform on $\mathbb{R}$ is Plancherel's theorem.
For square-integrable random variables, the conditional expectation $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is the orthogonal projection of $X$ onto the closed subspace of $\mathcal G$-measurable variables in $L^2$.

refs: Kreyszig, Introductory Functional Analysis with Applications
Brezis, Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and Partial Differential Equations
Young, An Introduction to Hilbert Space

blocks.body:
In the plane, the closest point of a line to a given point is found by dropping a perpendicular, and a vector is recovered from its components along perpendicular axes. A Fourier series does the same thing with functions: it writes $f$ as a sum of components along the "perpendicular axes" $\sin nx$ and $\cos nx$. To make that more than an analogy one needs a space in which functions have lengths and angles, and in which infinite sums of components actually converge.

That space is a Hilbert space: an inner product space that is complete. This page shows that in such a space the familiar geometry survives intact: perpendiculars exist and give best approximations, every continuous linear functional is an inner product, and orthonormal bases behave like coordinate axes.

blocks.title: Hilbert space
blocks.body:
An inner product on a vector space $H$ over $\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ (see [[inner-products]]) is a map $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:H\times H\to\mathbb{K}$ that is linear in the first variable, satisfies $\langle y,x\rangle=\overline{\langle x,y\rangle}$, and has $\langle x,x\rangle>0$ for $x\ne0$. It defines the norm $\|x\|=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$, which satisfies the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality $|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$ and hence the triangle inequality. A Hilbert space is an inner product space that is complete in this norm, that is, a [[normed-spaces|Banach space]] whose norm comes from an inner product.

Meaning: a Hilbert space is a possibly infinite-dimensional space with the full Euclidean toolkit of lengths, angles and perpendiculars, in which limits exist.

blocks.title: Examples and the parallelogram law
blocks.body:
The basic examples:

1. $\mathbb{C}^n$ with $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_ix_i\overline{y_i}$.
2. $\ell^2$, the square-summable sequences, with $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_nx_n\overline{y_n}$. The sum converges by Cauchy–Schwarz, and $\ell^2$ is complete.
3. $L^2[a,b]$, square-integrable functions (up to equality almost everywhere), with $\langle f,g\rangle=\int_a^bf\,\overline g$. Completeness here is the Riesz–Fischer theorem of [[lp-spaces]].

A non-example: $C[0,1]$ with $\langle f,g\rangle=\int_0^1f\,\overline g$ is an inner product space, but it is not complete; the continuous ramps that approach a step function form a Cauchy sequence with no continuous limit, as in the incomplete example on [[normed-spaces]]. Its completion is $L^2[0,1]$.

Expanding $\|x\pm y\|^2=\|x\|^2\pm2\operatorname{Re}\langle x,y\rangle+\|y\|^2$ and adding gives the parallelogram law
$$\|x+y\|^2+\|x-y\|^2=2\|x\|^2+2\|y\|^2 .$$
The sum of the squares of the diagonals of a parallelogram equals the sum of the squares of the four sides. The Jordan–von Neumann theorem (stated without proof) says the converse holds: a norm satisfying the parallelogram law comes from an inner product. So among the norms $\|\cdot\|_p$ only $p=2$ gives a Hilbert space. The parallelogram law is the one property the next proof uses.

blocks.title: Projection theorem
blocks.body:
Let $C$ be a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space $H$ and $x\in H$. There is exactly one point $c_0\in C$ with $\|x-c_0\|=\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|$.

If $C=M$ is a closed subspace, the nearest point $c_0=Px$ is characterised by $x-Px\perp M$; the map $P$ is linear with $\|P\|\le1$, and every $x$ splits uniquely as $x=Px+(x-Px)$ with $Px\in M$, $x-Px\in M^\perp$. That is, $H=M\oplus M^\perp$.

Let $d=\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|$ and pick $c_n\in C$ with $\|x-c_n\|\to d$. Apply the parallelogram law to $x-c_n$ and $x-c_m$:
$$\|c_n-c_m\|^2=2\|x-c_n\|^2+2\|x-c_m\|^2-4\Big\|x-\tfrac{c_n+c_m}{2}\Big\|^2 .$$
By convexity $\tfrac12(c_n+c_m)\in C$, so the last norm is at least $d$, and the right side is at most $2\|x-c_n\|^2+2\|x-c_m\|^2-4d^2\to0$. So $(c_n)$ is Cauchy. By completeness it converges, and since $C$ is closed the limit $c_0$ lies in $C$, with $\|x-c_0\|=d$. If $c_0'$ is another minimiser, the same identity with $c_0,c_0'$ in place of $c_n,c_m$ gives $\|c_0-c_0'\|^2\le4d^2-4d^2=0$.

Now let $C=M$ be a closed subspace and $c_0$ the minimiser. For $m\in M$ and real $t$, $c_0+tm\in M$, so
$$\|x-c_0-tm\|^2-\|x-c_0\|^2=-2t\operatorname{Re}\langle x-c_0,m\rangle+t^2\|m\|^2\ge0$$
for all $t$, which forces $\operatorname{Re}\langle x-c_0,m\rangle=0$. Replacing $m$ by $im$ in the complex case gives $\langle x-c_0,m\rangle=0$. So $x-c_0\perp M$. Conversely, if $c\in M$ and $x-c\perp M$, then for any $m\in M$ Pythagoras gives $\|x-m\|^2=\|x-c\|^2+\|c-m\|^2\ge\|x-c\|^2$, so $c$ is the minimiser. The characterisation shows that $P$ is linear (if $x-Px\perp M$ and $y-Py\perp M$ then $(x+y)-(Px+Py)\perp M$), and Pythagoras gives $\|x\|^2=\|Px\|^2+\|x-Px\|^2$, so $\|Px\|\le\|x\|$. Uniqueness of the splitting holds because $M\cap M^\perp=\{0\}$.

blocks.title: Orthonormal bases
blocks.body:
A family $(e_n)$ is orthonormal if $\langle e_n,e_m\rangle$ is $1$ for $n=m$ and $0$ otherwise. For finitely many, the projection onto their span is $x\mapsto\sum_{n\le N}\langle x,e_n\rangle e_n$, and Pythagoras gives
$$\Big\|x-\sum_{n\le N}\langle x,e_n\rangle e_n\Big\|^2=\|x\|^2-\sum_{n\le N}|\langle x,e_n\rangle|^2 .$$
Since the left side is at least $0$, letting $N\to\infty$ gives Bessel's inequality $\sum_n|\langle x,e_n\rangle|^2\le\|x\|^2$. Also, for any scalars $(c_n)$ the series $\sum c_ne_n$ converges if and only if $\sum|c_n|^2< \infty$, because $\|\sum_{N< n\le M}c_ne_n\|^2=\sum_{N< n\le M}|c_n|^2$ and $H$ is complete.

An orthonormal sequence is called complete, or an orthonormal basis, if it satisfies the equivalent conditions of the next theorem. By applying Gram–Schmidt to a dense sequence, every separable Hilbert space has a countable orthonormal basis, and the map $x\mapsto(\langle x,e_n\rangle)_n$ is then an isometric isomorphism onto $\ell^2$ (or onto $\mathbb{K}^N$ if $\dim H=N$). So, up to isomorphism, there is only one infinite-dimensional separable Hilbert space. Note that "basis" here allows infinite sums; it is not a basis in the algebraic sense of [[basis-dimension]].

blocks.title: Characterisations of an orthonormal basis

blocks.body:
(1 ⇒ 2) By Bessel's inequality the series $s=\sum_n\langle x,e_n\rangle e_n$ converges. By continuity of the inner product, $\langle x-s,e_m\rangle=\langle x,e_m\rangle-\langle x,e_m\rangle=0$ for each $m$, so $x-s=0$ by (1).

(2 ⇒ 3) Let $N\to\infty$ in the displayed Pythagoras identity: the left side tends to $0$.

(3 ⇒ 4) The same identity shows that the finite sums $\sum_{n\le N}\langle x,e_n\rangle e_n$, which lie in the span, converge to $x$.

(4 ⇒ 1) If $x\perp e_n$ for all $n$, then $x$ is orthogonal to the span and, by continuity, to its closure, which is $H$. So $\langle x,x\rangle=0$ and $x=0$.

blocks.title: A best approximation
blocks.body: Find the straight line $a+bx$ closest to $x^2$ in $L^2[0,1]$, that is, minimising $\int_0^1(x^2-a-bx)^2\,dx$, and compute the minimum.
blocks.solution:
The lines form the closed (finite-dimensional) subspace $M=\operatorname{span}\{1,x\}$. By the projection theorem the minimiser is characterised by $x^2-a-bx\perp1$ and $\perp x$:
$$\int_0^1(x^2-a-bx)\,dx=\tfrac13-a-\tfrac b2=0,\qquad \int_0^1(x^2-a-bx)\,x\,dx=\tfrac14-\tfrac a2-\tfrac b3=0 .$$
From the first, $a=\tfrac13-\tfrac b2$; substituting into the second gives $\tfrac1{12}-\tfrac b{12}=0$, so $b=1$ and $a=-\tfrac16$. The error is
$$\int_0^1\Big(x^2-x+\tfrac16\Big)^2dx=\frac1{180}.$$
These are the normal equations of [[least-squares]], with sums replaced by integrals. The residual $x^2-x+\frac16$ is, up to a constant factor, the second Legendre polynomial on $[0,1]$.

blocks.title: Parseval and the Basel sum
blocks.body: The functions $e_n(x)=e^{inx}/\sqrt{2\pi}$, $n\in\mathbb{Z}$, form an orthonormal basis of $L^2[-\pi,\pi]$ (orthonormality is a direct computation; completeness is a theorem from [[fourier-series]]). Apply Parseval's identity to $f(x)=x$ to find $\sum_{n\ge1}1/n^2$.
blocks.solution:
For $n\ne0$, integration by parts gives
$$\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}x\,e^{-inx}\,dx=\Big[\frac{x\,e^{-inx}}{-in}\Big]_{-\pi}^{\pi}+\frac1{in}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}e^{-inx}\,dx=\frac{2\pi(-1)^n}{-in}+0=\frac{2\pi i\,(-1)^n}{n},$$
and for $n=0$ the integral is $0$ because $x$ is odd. So $\langle f,e_n\rangle=\frac{2\pi i(-1)^n}{n\sqrt{2\pi}}$ and $|\langle f,e_n\rangle|^2=\frac{2\pi}{n^2}$. On the other side $\|f\|^2=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}x^2\,dx=\frac{2\pi^3}{3}$. Parseval gives
$$\frac{2\pi^3}{3}=\sum_{n\ne0}\frac{2\pi}{n^2}=4\pi\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1{n^2},\qquad\text{so}\qquad\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1{n^2}=\frac{\pi^2}{6}.$$

blocks.title: Many vectors pointing away from each other
blocks.body: In a real Hilbert space of any dimension, possibly infinite, let $u_1,\dots,u_n$ be unit vectors with $\langle u_i,u_j\rangle\le-c$ for all $i\ne j$, where $c>0$. Show that $n\le1+\frac1c$, and that the bound is attained when $1/c$ is an integer.
blocks.solution:
The only inequality needed is $\|v\|^2\ge0$ for $v=u_1+\cdots+u_n$:
$$0\le\Big\|\sum_iu_i\Big\|^2=\sum_i\|u_i\|^2+\sum_{i\ne j}\langle u_i,u_j\rangle\le n-n(n-1)c .$$
Dividing by $n$ gives $1-(n-1)c\ge0$, that is $n\le1+1/c$. The dimension of the space never entered.

If $1/c=k$ is an integer, take the $k+1$ vertices of a regular simplex centred at the origin in $\mathbb{R}^k$, scaled to unit length; their pairwise inner products are exactly $-1/k$, and $k+1=1+1/c$. For example, with $c=\frac12$ the bound is $3$, attained by three unit vectors at $120^\circ$ in the plane.

blocks.body:
- An orthonormal basis of an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is not a basis in the linear-algebra sense: most vectors are infinite sums $\sum c_ne_n$, not finite combinations.
- The projection theorem needs both completeness and closedness. Onto a non-closed subspace, such as the finitely supported sequences in $\ell^2$, a nearest point may not exist.
- The Riesz theorem fails without completeness. On the space of finitely supported sequences with the $\ell^2$ inner product, $f(x)=\sum_nx_n/n$ is bounded, but the only candidate $y=(1,\tfrac12,\tfrac13,\dots)$ is not in that space.
- $\|e_n\|=1$ for all $n$, yet $\langle e_n,y\rangle\to0$ for every fixed $y$ (by Bessel). So $e_n$ tends to $0$ weakly but not in norm; bounded sequences need not have norm-convergent subsequences.
- Conventions: mathematicians usually make $\langle x,y\rangle$ linear in $x$; physicists' bra-ket $\langle x|y\rangle$ is linear in $y$. Formulas such as the one for $y$ in the Riesz proof change by a conjugation.

The prerequisites are [[normed-spaces]] and [[inner-products]]; the finite-dimensional [[spectral-theorem]] is the model for what comes next. The main continuation is the theory of [[compact-operators]], where self-adjoint compact operators on a Hilbert space have an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, which is the abstract form of eigenfunction expansions in [[sturm-liouville]] problems and of separation of variables for the [[heat-equation]] and [[wave-equation]]. Riesz representation makes the dual of a Hilbert space a copy of the space itself, which makes the [[hahn-banach]] theorem easy in this setting. In quantum mechanics, states are unit vectors in a Hilbert space and observables are self-adjoint operators; the Fourier transform is a unitary map on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ (see [[fourier-transform]]).

1. Show that the orthogonal complement $A^\perp$ of any subset $A\subseteq H$ is a closed subspace, and that $(M^\perp)^\perp=M$ for a closed subspace $M$.
2. Find the projection of $x=(1,1,1,\dots,1,0,0,\dots)$ (with $N$ ones) onto the closed subspace $\{y\in\ell^2:y_1=y_2\}$.
3. Find the bounded linear functional on $L^2[0,1]$ represented by $y(t)=t$, and compute its norm.
4. Use Parseval for $f(x)=x^2$ on $[-\pi,\pi]$ to find $\sum_{n\ge1}1/n^4$.

Brezis, Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and Partial Differential Equations
