entry.sum: The Hahn–Banach theorem says that a linear functional dominated by a sublinear function on a subspace extends to the whole space with the same domination; in a normed space, every bounded functional on a subspace extends to the whole space with the same norm. Its consequences are that the dual space $X^*$ separates points, that $\|x\|=\max_{\|f\|\le1}|f(x)|$, and, in geometric form, that disjoint convex sets (one of them open) can be separated by a closed hyperplane.
key: f\le p \text{ on } M,\ p \text{ sublinear} \ \Longrightarrow\ \exists F \text{ linear on } X:\ F|_M=f,\ F\le p
entry.why: Without it the dual space of a general normed space could be trivial and duality arguments would be empty; with it one gets weak topologies, the bidual embedding, separation of convex sets (the basis of duality in optimisation) and existence results such as Banach limits.

links.note: The separation form underlies duality in convex optimisation: Farkas' lemma, Lagrange multipliers for convex programs and the KKT conditions all come from separating a convex set from a point or another convex set.

In full generality the theorem is not provable in ZF alone, but it follows from the ultrafilter lemma (equivalently the Boolean prime ideal theorem), which is strictly weaker than the axiom of choice; in reverse mathematics, Brown and Simpson showed that over $\mathsf{RCA}_0$ the Hahn–Banach theorem for separable Banach spaces is equivalent to $\mathsf{WKL}_0$.

refs: Brezis, Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and Partial Differential Equations
Kreyszig, Introductory Functional Analysis with Applications
Folland, Real Analysis: Modern Techniques and Their Applications

blocks.body:
In finite dimensions, linear functionals are everywhere: on $\mathbb{R}^n$ every linear map to $\mathbb{R}$ is $x\mapsto a\cdot x$, they are all continuous, and they are plentiful enough to tell any two points apart. On an infinite-dimensional normed space $X$ it is not obvious that there is even one nonzero continuous linear functional. The dual space $X^*$ (see [[dual-spaces]]) is only useful if it is big.

The Hahn–Banach theorem settles this. Its analytic form is an extension theorem: a functional defined on a subspace, and controlled there by a convex size function, can be extended to the whole space with the same control. Its geometric form is a separation theorem for convex sets. Together they make duality a working tool in [[normed-spaces]] and beyond.

blocks.title: A two-dimensional warm-up
Sublinear functional
blocks.body:
On a real vector space $X$, a function $p:X\to\mathbb{R}$ is sublinear if $p(x+y)\le p(x)+p(y)$ and $p(tx)=t\,p(x)$ for all $x,y\in X$ and $t\ge0$.

Examples: any norm or seminorm; $C\|x\|$ for a constant $C\ge0$; the Minkowski gauge $p_C(x)=\inf\{t>0:x/t\in C\}$ of a convex set $C$ containing a ball around $0$; and on bounded sequences, $p(x)=\limsup_n x_n$. Meaning: a sublinear functional is a one-sided, possibly asymmetric, notion of size.

blocks.title: Hahn–Banach theorem (dominated extension)
blocks.body: Let $X$ be a real vector space, $p$ a sublinear functional on $X$, $M\subseteq X$ a subspace and $f:M\to\mathbb{R}$ linear with $f(m)\le p(m)$ for all $m\in M$. Then there is a linear $F:X\to\mathbb{R}$ with $F|_M=f$ and $F(x)\le p(x)$ for all $x\in X$.

Step 1: one more dimension. Suppose $x_0\notin M$ and let $M_1=M+\mathbb{R}x_0$. Any linear extension has the form $F(m+tx_0)=f(m)+ta$ for some number $a$, and we need $f(m)+ta\le p(m+tx_0)$ for all $m\in M$, $t\in\mathbb{R}$. For $t=0$ this is the hypothesis. For $t>0$, divide by $t$ and rename $m/t$ as $m$: the condition becomes $a\le p(m+x_0)-f(m)$ for all $m\in M$. For $t<0$, divide by $|t|$: it becomes $a\ge f(m')-p(m'-x_0)$ for all $m'\in M$. So a suitable $a$ exists exactly when
$$f(m')-p(m'-x_0)\le p(m+x_0)-f(m)\quad\text{for all } m,m'\in M .$$
This holds, because $$f(m)+f(m')=f(m+m')\le p(m+m')\le p(m+x_0)+p(m'-x_0)$$. Choose $a$ between the supremum of the left sides and the infimum of the right sides.

Step 2: all dimensions at once. Let $\mathcal P$ be the set of pairs $(N,g)$ with $N$ a subspace containing $M$, $g$ linear on $N$, $g|_M=f$ and $g\le p$ on $N$. Order it by $(N,g)\preceq(N',g')$ when $N\subseteq N'$ and $g'|_N=g$. A chain in $\mathcal P$ has an upper bound: the union of the subspaces, with the common extension of the functionals. By Zorn's lemma (see [[ordinals-cardinals]] for the axiom of choice) there is a maximal element $(N,g)$. If $N\ne X$, Step 1 would extend $g$ to $N+\mathbb{R}x_0$ for some $x_0\notin N$, contradicting maximality. So $N=X$ and $F=g$ works.

When $X$ is a separable normed space and $p$ is continuous, Zorn can be avoided: apply Step 1 along a dense sequence and extend to the closure by continuity.

blocks.title: Hahn–Banach theorem for normed spaces
blocks.body: Let $X$ be a real or complex normed space, $M$ a subspace and $g:M\to\mathbb{K}$ a bounded linear functional. Then there is $G\in X^*$ with $G|_M=g$ and $\|G\|=\|g\|$.

Real case. Apply the previous theorem with $p(x)=\|g\|\,\|x\|$, which is sublinear. The extension satisfies $G(x)\le\|g\|\,\|x\|$ and $-G(x)=G(-x)\le\|g\|\,\|x\|$, so $|G(x)|\le\|g\|\,\|x\|$ and $\|G\|\le\|g\|$; the reverse inequality is automatic because $G$ extends $g$.

Complex case. Let $u=\operatorname{Re}g$, a real-linear functional on $M$ with $|u(x)|\le\|g\|\,\|x\|$. Since $\operatorname{Im}g(x)=-\operatorname{Re}(ig(x))=-u(ix)$, we have $g(x)=u(x)-iu(ix)$. Extend $u$ by the real case to a real-linear $U$ on $X$ with $|U(x)|\le\|g\|\,\|x\|$ and put $G(x)=U(x)-iU(ix)$. A direct check shows $G(ix)=iG(x)$, so $G$ is complex-linear, and $G$ extends $g$. For the norm, given $x$ choose $|\lambda|=1$ with $\lambda G(x)=|G(x)|$. Then $|G(x)|=G(\lambda x)$ is real, so it equals its real part $U(\lambda x)\le\|g\|\,\|\lambda x\|=\|g\|\,\|x\|$.

blocks.title: Consequences for the dual space
blocks.body:
1. Norming functionals. For $x_0\ne0$ there is $f\in X^*$ with $\|f\|=1$ and $f(x_0)=\|x_0\|$: define $f(tx_0)=t\|x_0\|$ on $\mathbb{K}x_0$, which has norm $1$, and extend. Hence $X^*$ separates points (if $x\ne y$ some $f$ has $f(x)\ne f(y)$), and $\|x\|=\max_{\|f\|\le1}|f(x)|$, the maximum being attained.
2. The bidual. The map $J:X\to X^{\ast\ast}$, $J(x)(f)=f(x)$, is linear, and by (1) it is an isometry. $X$ is called reflexive if $J$ is onto. The spaces $\ell^p$ and $L^p$ with $1< p< \infty$, and all Hilbert spaces, are reflexive; $\ell^1$, $\ell^\infty$, $c_0$ and $C[0,1]$ are not.
3. Annihilators and closures. If $M$ is a closed subspace and $x_0\notin M$ with $\delta=\operatorname{dist}(x_0,M)>0$, there is $f\in X^*$ with $\|f\|=1$, $f|_M=0$ and $f(x_0)=\delta$. (On $M+\mathbb{K}x_0$ set $g(m+tx_0)=t\delta$; then $|g(m+tx_0)|=|t|\delta\le\|m+tx_0\|$, so $\|g\|\le1$, and extend.) Consequently a point lies in the closure of a subspace $M$ exactly when every functional vanishing on $M$ vanishes at that point, and $\operatorname{dist}(x_0,M)=\max\{|f(x_0)|:\|f\|\le1,\ f|_M=0\}$.

Some duals, stated without proof, with $1/p+1/q=1$: $(\ell^p)^*\cong\ell^q$ for $1\le p< \infty$, $(c_0)^*\cong\ell^1$, and $(\ell^1)^*\cong\ell^\infty$. The dual of $\ell^\infty$ is strictly larger than $\ell^1$; the Banach limit example below exhibits an element not of the form $x\mapsto\sum a_nx_n$.

blocks.title: Separation of convex sets
blocks.body:
Let $X$ be a real normed space and $A,B\subseteq X$ disjoint nonempty convex sets.

1. If $A$ is open, there are $f\in X^*$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ with $f(a)< \alpha\le f(b)$ for all $a\in A$, $b\in B$.
2. If $A$ is closed and $B$ is compact, there is $f\in X^*$ with $\sup_Af< \inf_Bf$.

blocks.title: Proof sketch
blocks.body:
For (1), first separate an open convex set $C$ from a point $x_0\notin C$. Translate so that $0\in C$; then $C$ contains a ball $\{\|x\|< r\}$ and its gauge $p_C$ is sublinear with $p_C(x)\le\|x\|/r$, while $C=\{p_C<1\}$ because $C$ is open, and $p_C(x_0)\ge1$. On $\mathbb{R}x_0$ put $g(tx_0)=t$; then $g\le p_C$ there (for $t\le0$ trivially, for $t>0$ since $p_C(tx_0)=t\,p_C(x_0)\ge t$). Extend to $F\le p_C$ on $X$. Then $F$ is bounded by $\|x\|/r$, $F(x_0)=1$ and $F<1$ on $C$. For general $A,B$ apply this to the open convex set $C=A-B=\{a-b\}$, which does not contain $0$: we get $F(a)< F(b)$ for all $a,b$, and $\alpha=\inf_BF$ works, with strict inequality on $A$ because $F(A)$ is an open interval.

For (2), $\inf\{\|a-b\|\}=\varepsilon>0$ by compactness of $B$ and closedness of $A$, so $A_\varepsilon=A+\{\|x\|< \varepsilon/2\}$ and $B_\varepsilon=B+\{\|x\|< \varepsilon/2\}$ are disjoint open convex sets. Separating them by (1) and using that each contains a ball around every point of $A$, respectively $B$, gives a strict gap.

blocks.title: Distances by duality
blocks.body: In $\mathbb{R}^3$ let $M$ be the plane $x_1+x_2+x_3=0$ and $x_0=(1,2,3)$. Find $\operatorname{dist}(x_0,M)$ for the norms $\|\cdot\|_1$, $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ and $\|\cdot\|_2$, and a nearest point in each case.
blocks.solution:
Here $M=\ker g$ with $g(x)=x_1+x_2+x_3$, and the functionals vanishing on $M$ are the multiples of $g$. By consequence 3 above, $\operatorname{dist}(x_0,M)=\max_{|s|\,\|g\|\le1}|s\,g(x_0)|=|g(x_0)|/\|g\|$, where $\|g\|$ is the dual norm of $(1,1,1)$. Here $g(x_0)=6$.

- For $\|\cdot\|_1$, the dual norm is $\|\cdot\|_\infty$, so $\|g\|=1$ and the distance is $6$. A nearest point is $m=(1,2,-3)$, with $x_0-m=(0,0,6)$.
- For $\|\cdot\|_\infty$, $\|g\|=\|(1,1,1)\|_1=3$ and the distance is $2$. A nearest point is $m=(-1,0,1)$, with $x_0-m=(2,2,2)$.
- For $\|\cdot\|_2$, $\|g\|=\sqrt3$ and the distance is $6/\sqrt3=2\sqrt3$, attained at the orthogonal projection $m=x_0-2(1,1,1)=(-1,0,1)$.

In this finite-dimensional case the duality formula can be checked by hand or by linear programming; its value is that the same formula, with $\max$ over annihilating functionals, holds for every closed subspace of every normed space.

blocks.title: Banach limits
blocks.body: On the space $\ell^\infty$ of bounded real sequences let $S$ be the shift $(Sx)_n=x_{n+1}$. Show that there is a linear functional $L$ on $\ell^\infty$ with $L(x)=\lim x_n$ whenever the limit exists, $L(Sx)=L(x)$, and $\liminf x_n\le L(x)\le\limsup x_n$. Compute $L$ on $(1,0,1,0,\dots)$ and on $(1,0,0,1,0,0,\dots)$.
blocks.solution:
Let $p(x)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{x_1+\cdots+x_n}{n}$. It is sublinear, and on the subspace $c$ of convergent sequences the Cesàro averages converge to $\lim x_n$, so $f(x)=\lim x_n$ satisfies $f=p$ on $c$. Hahn–Banach gives a linear $L$ on $\ell^\infty$ extending $f$ with $L\le p$.

Bounds: $L(x)\le p(x)\le\limsup x_n$, and $-L(x)=L(-x)\le p(-x)\le-\liminf x_n$.

Shift invariance: the averages of $Sx-x$ telescope, $\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^n(x_{k+1}-x_k)=\frac{x_{n+1}-x_1}{n}\to0$ because $x$ is bounded. So $p(Sx-x)=0$ and also $p(x-Sx)=0$, which give $L(Sx)-L(x)\le0$ and $L(x)-L(Sx)\le0$.

For $x=(1,0,1,0,\dots)$, $x+Sx=(1,1,1,\dots)$, so $2L(x)=1$ and $L(x)=\frac12$. For the period-$3$ sequence $y=(1,0,0,1,0,0,\dots)$, $y+Sy+S^2y=(1,1,1,\dots)$, so $L(y)=\frac13$. These values are forced for every Banach limit, though $L$ itself is not unique and no explicit formula for it is known.

Finally, $L$ is not of the form $x\mapsto\sum a_nx_n$ with $a\in\ell^1$: such a functional would give $a_n=L(e_n)=\lim(e_n)=0$ for all $n$, hence $L=0$, while $L(1,1,1,\dots)=1$.

blocks.body:
- Extensions are generally not unique (the $\|\cdot\|_1$ warm-up). Uniqueness of norm-preserving extensions holds in Hilbert spaces, where the extension is given by the Riesz representation and is zero on $M^\perp$.
- The theorem extends functionals, not operators. The identity map of $c_0$ has no bounded linear extension to a map $\ell^\infty\to c_0$ (Phillips' theorem, stated without proof), so $c_0$ is not complemented in $\ell^\infty$.
- Separation needs some interior. In $\ell^2$ the set $C$ of finitely supported sequences whose last nonzero entry is positive is convex, dense, and does not contain $0$; any continuous $f$ with $f\ge f(0)=0$ on $C$ is $\ge0$ on the closure $\ell^2$, so $f=0$. The point $0$ and $C$ cannot be separated.
- For complex spaces, the dominated version is about real parts. Applying the real theorem to a complex functional directly does not produce a complex-linear extension; the $u(x)-iu(ix)$ construction is needed.
- The general theorem uses Zorn's lemma, so it produces functionals (such as Banach limits) that cannot be written down explicitly.

The page assumes [[normed-spaces]] and [[dual-spaces]]. In [[hilbert-spaces]] the Riesz representation theorem makes the extension trivial: project onto the closure of $M$ and use the representing vector. Hahn–Banach is one of the pillars of functional analysis together with the uniform boundedness principle, the open mapping theorem and the closed graph theorem; it is what makes the weak topology on $X$ Hausdorff (because $X^*$ separates points), and it is used to show that the adjoint of an operator has the same norm as the operator, a fact used throughout the theory of [[compact-operators]]. Its finite-dimensional separation form is the basis of duality in [[linear-programming]] and [[convex-optimisation]], and in [[lp-spaces]] it is used to identify duals and to show that $L^\infty$ has a dual larger than $L^1$.

1. Show that $p(x)=\limsup_n x_n$ is sublinear on $\ell^\infty$, and that it is not linear.
2. In $(\mathbb{R}^2,\|\cdot\|_1)$, describe all norm-one functionals $f$ with $f(1,1)=2$. How many are there in $(\mathbb{R}^2,\|\cdot\|_\infty)$ with $f(1,1)=1$?
3. Let $X$ be a normed space with $X^*$ separable. Using consequence 3, show that $X$ is separable.
4. Show that the Banach limit constructed in the example satisfies $L(x)=\lim_n\frac{x_1+\cdots+x_n}{n}$ whenever that limit exists, and give a bounded sequence whose Cesàro averages do not converge.

entry.sum: A bounded operator between Banach spaces is compact if it maps bounded sets to sets with compact closure; examples are finite-rank operators, their norm limits, and integral operators with continuous or square-integrable kernels. Compact operators behave like matrices: a compact self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors with eigenvalues tending to $0$, and for $\lambda\ne0$ the Fredholm alternative holds: $Tu-\lambda u=f$ is solvable for every $f$ exactly when $Tu=\lambda u$ has only the solution $u=0$.
entry.why: Boundary value problems and integral equations are usually turned into equations $u-\lambda Tu=f$ with $T$ compact; the Fredholm alternative then gives existence from uniqueness, and the spectral theorem gives eigenfunction expansions such as Fourier series and the vibration modes of a drum.

links.note: A regular Sturm–Liouville problem is inverted by an integral operator with a continuous symmetric Green's function, which is compact and self-adjoint, so its eigenfunctions form an orthonormal basis of $L^2$.
Nyström and Galerkin methods replace a compact integral operator by finite-rank approximations, and convergence of the approximate solutions rests on compactness and the Fredholm alternative.

Quantum Hamiltonians with compact resolvent, such as a particle in a box or the harmonic oscillator, have purely discrete energy levels, given by the spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators.

blocks.body:
For an $n\times n$ matrix $A$ and a number $\lambda$, linear algebra gives a clean dichotomy: either $Au-\lambda u=f$ has exactly one solution for every $f$, or $Au=\lambda u$ has a nonzero solution, and in the second case $Au-\lambda u=f$ is solvable only for $f$ in a proper subspace. Integral equations such as
$$u(x)-\lambda\int_0^1K(x,y)\,u(y)\,dy=f(x)$$
are linear equations in an infinite-dimensional space, and for general operators that dichotomy breaks down. Fredholm discovered around 1900 that for integral operators of this kind it survives.

The reason is compactness. A compact operator squeezes the infinite-dimensional unit ball into something that is almost finite-dimensional, and that is enough to rescue most of matrix theory: the dichotomy (the Fredholm alternative) and diagonalisation of symmetric operators (the spectral theorem). This page assumes [[hilbert-spaces]], the finite-dimensional [[spectral-theorem]] and the [[arzela-ascoli]] theorem.

blocks.title: Compact operator
blocks.body:
Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces. A linear operator $T:X\to Y$ is compact if the image $T(B)$ of the closed unit ball $B$ of $X$ has compact closure in $Y$. Equivalently, for every bounded sequence $(x_n)$ in $X$ the sequence $(Tx_n)$ has a convergent subsequence. Compact operators are bounded, since a set with compact closure is bounded.

Meaning: $T$ is compact when it destroys all but a "finite-dimensional amount" of the infinitely many independent directions in $X$.

blocks.title: Examples and non-examples
blocks.body:
1. Finite-rank operators. If $T$ is bounded and $T(X)$ is finite-dimensional, then $T(B)$ is a bounded subset of a finite-dimensional space, whose closure is compact. So every matrix, and every operator $Tu=\sum_{i\le N}\varphi_i(u)\,y_i$ with $\varphi_i\in X^*$, is compact.
2. The identity on an infinite-dimensional space is not compact. In a Hilbert space an orthonormal sequence $(e_n)$ is bounded, but $\|e_n-e_m\|=\sqrt2$ for $n\ne m$, so no subsequence converges. More generally, by Riesz's lemma the unit ball of a normed space is compact only in finite dimensions. Consequently a compact operator on an infinite-dimensional space is never invertible: if $T^{-1}$ were bounded, $I=T^{-1}T$ would be compact.
3. Diagonal operators. On $\ell^2$, the operator $De_n=\mu_ne_n$ with $\mu_n\to0$ is compact. Its truncation $D_N$ (keep $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_N$, set the rest to $0$) has finite rank, and $\|D-D_N\|=\sup_{n>N}|\mu_n|\to0$. With $\mu_n=1/n$ this gives $\|D-D_N\|=1/(N+1)$. If $\mu_n\not\to0$, there are infinitely many $n$ with $|\mu_n|\ge\delta>0$, and $De_n$ along those $n$ has no convergent subsequence, so $D$ is not compact.
4. Integral operators. If $K$ is continuous on $[0,1]^2$, then $(Ku)(x)=\int_0^1K(x,y)u(y)\,dy$ is compact on $C[0,1]$ with the sup norm. For $\|u\|_\infty\le1$ we have $|Ku(x)|\le\max|K|$ and $|Ku(x)-Ku(x')|\le\max_y|K(x,y)-K(x',y)|$, which is small when $|x-x'|$ is small, by uniform continuity of $K$. So the image of the unit ball is bounded and equicontinuous, and Arzelà–Ascoli says its closure is compact. On $L^2[0,1]$ the same operator is compact whenever $\int\!\!\int|K|^2< \infty$ (a Hilbert–Schmidt operator), and then $\|K\|\le(\int\!\!\int|K|^2)^{1/2}$.

blocks.title: Compact operators form a closed ideal
blocks.body: Let $X,Y,Z$ be Banach spaces. Sums and scalar multiples of compact operators $X\to Y$ are compact; if $T$ is compact and $S$ is bounded, then $ST$ and $TS$ are compact whenever defined; and if $T_n\to T$ in operator norm with each $T_n$ compact, then $T$ is compact. In particular every norm limit of finite-rank operators is compact. In a Hilbert space the converse holds: every compact operator is a norm limit of finite-rank operators.

blocks.title: Proof of the closedness statement
blocks.body:
A subset of the complete space $Y$ has compact closure if and only if it is totally bounded: for every $\varepsilon>0$ it is covered by finitely many balls of radius $\varepsilon$. Let $\varepsilon>0$ and pick $n$ with $\|T-T_n\|< \varepsilon/3$. Since $T_n(B)$ is totally bounded there are $x_1,\dots,x_k\in B$ such that every $T_nx$, $x\in B$, is within $\varepsilon/3$ of some $T_nx_i$. Then
$$\|Tx-Tx_i\|\le\|Tx-T_nx\|+\|T_nx-T_nx_i\|+\|T_nx_i-Tx_i\|< \varepsilon,$$
so the balls of radius $\varepsilon$ about $Tx_1,\dots,Tx_k$ cover $T(B)$. Hence $T(B)$ is totally bounded and $T$ is compact. The other closure properties follow directly from the sequence definition. For the Hilbert-space converse, if $P_N$ is the orthogonal projection onto the span of the first $N$ vectors of an orthonormal basis of the closure of $T(H)$ (which is separable), then $P_NT$ has finite rank and $\|T-P_NT\|\to0$; the proof uses compactness of the closure of $T(B)$ and is omitted.

blocks.title: Spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators
blocks.body:
Let $T$ be a compact self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space $H$. Then there is an orthonormal sequence $(e_n)$, finite or infinite, of eigenvectors with nonzero real eigenvalues $\lambda_n$, $|\lambda_1|\ge|\lambda_2|\ge\cdots$, such that
$$Tx=\sum_n\lambda_n\langle x,e_n\rangle e_n\quad\text{for all }x\in H .$$
If the sequence is infinite then $\lambda_n\to0$. Each nonzero eigenvalue has finite multiplicity, and $H$ is the orthogonal direct sum of $\ker T$ and the closed span of the $e_n$.

blocks.title: Proof sketch
blocks.body:
Key step: if $T\ne0$, then $\|T\|$ or $-\|T\|$ is an eigenvalue. For self-adjoint $T$ one has $\|T\|=\sup_{\|x\|=1}|\langle Tx,x\rangle|$ (a standard lemma), so there are unit vectors $x_n$ with $\langle Tx_n,x_n\rangle\to\lambda$, where $\lambda=\pm\|T\|$. Then
$$\|Tx_n-\lambda x_n\|^2=\|Tx_n\|^2-2\lambda\langle Tx_n,x_n\rangle+\lambda^2\le2\lambda^2-2\lambda\langle Tx_n,x_n\rangle\to0 .$$
By compactness a subsequence has $Tx_n\to y$; then $\lambda x_n=Tx_n-(Tx_n-\lambda x_n)\to y$, so $x_n\to e=y/\lambda$, a unit vector with $Te=\lambda e$.

Iteration: $T$ maps $e^\perp$ into itself (if $x\perp e$ then $\langle Tx,e\rangle=\langle x,Te\rangle=\lambda\langle x,e\rangle=0$), and its restriction there is again compact and self-adjoint with norm at most $|\lambda|$. Repeating produces $e_1,e_2,\dots$ with $|\lambda_1|\ge|\lambda_2|\ge\cdots$, stopping if the restriction becomes $0$. If infinitely many $|\lambda_n|\ge\delta>0$, then $\|Te_n-Te_m\|^2=\lambda_n^2+\lambda_m^2\ge2\delta^2$, contradicting compactness; so $\lambda_n\to0$, and each nonzero eigenvalue occurs only finitely often. Finally, let $W$ be the orthogonal complement of all the $e_n$. It is invariant under $T$, and the restriction of $T$ to $W$ is $0$: if the process stopped, by construction; otherwise its norm is at most $|\lambda_{n+1}|$ for every $n$, which tends to $0$. Writing $x=\sum_n\langle x,e_n\rangle e_n+w$ with $w\in W$ gives the expansion. So $W\subseteq\ker T$, and $\ker T\subseteq W$ because eigenvectors for $\lambda_n\ne0$ are orthogonal to $\ker T$; this gives the decomposition.

blocks.title: Fredholm alternative
Proof of parts 1–3
blocks.body:
Part 1. On $N=\ker A$ we have $T=\lambda I$. If $(x_n)$ is a bounded sequence in $N$, a subsequence of $Tx_n=\lambda x_n$ converges, so a subsequence of $x_n$ converges (in $N$, which is closed). The unit ball of $N$ is therefore compact, and $N$ is finite-dimensional by Riesz's lemma.

Part 2, closed range. First, there is $c>0$ with $\|Au\|\ge c\|u\|$ for all $u\perp N$. Otherwise there are unit vectors $u_n\perp N$ with $Au_n\to0$. Pass to a subsequence with $Tu_n\to v$. Then $\lambda u_n=Tu_n-Au_n\to v$, so $u_n\to u=v/\lambda$, with $\|u\|=1$, $u\perp N$ and $Au=\lim Au_n=0$, so $u\in N$: a contradiction. Now if $Au_n\to f$, write $u_n=w_n+z_n$ with $z_n\in N$ and $w_n\perp N$; then $Aw_n=Au_n$ and $\|w_n-w_m\|\le\|Aw_n-Aw_m\|/c$, so $(w_n)$ is Cauchy, converges to some $w$, and $Aw=f$. The identity $A(H)=\ker(A^*)^\perp$ holds for every bounded operator with closed range, because $\langle Au,v\rangle=\langle u,A^*v\rangle$ shows $A(H)^\perp=\ker A^*$.

Part 3, injective implies surjective. Suppose $\ker A=\{0\}$ but $H_1=A(H)\ne H$. Set $H_k=A^k(H)$. Each $A^k=(-\lambda)^kI+(\text{compact})$ by the binomial theorem, so by part 2 each $H_k$ is closed, and $H_{k+1}\subseteq H_k$. The inclusions are strict: if $H_{k+1}=H_k$ then for any $u$, $A^ku=A^{k+1}w$ for some $w$, so $u=Aw$ by injectivity of $A^k$, giving $H_1=H$. Choose unit vectors $x_k\in H_k$ with $x_k\perp H_{k+1}$. For $k< m$,
$$Tx_k-Tx_m=\lambda x_k+\big(Ax_k-Ax_m-\lambda x_m\big),$$
and the bracket lies in $H_{k+1}$, which is orthogonal to $x_k$. So $\|Tx_k-Tx_m\|\ge|\lambda|$ for all $k< m$, and $(Tx_k)$ has no convergent subsequence, contradicting compactness.

Surjective implies injective. If $A(H)=H$ then $\ker A^*=A(H)^\perp=\{0\}$. Since $T^*$ is also compact (a standard fact), the previous paragraph applied to $A^*$ gives $A^*(H)=H$, and then $\ker A=A^*(H)^\perp=\{0\}$. Part 4 is proved by a finite-dimensional reduction and is omitted here.

blocks.title: A rank-one integral equation
blocks.body: Solve $u(x)-\lambda\int_0^1xy\,u(y)\,dy=f(x)$ on $[0,1]$ for continuous $f$, and explain the answer with the Fredholm alternative. In particular, find $u$ when $\lambda=1$ and $f\equiv1$.
blocks.solution:
Write $c=\int_0^1y\,u(y)\,dy$, a number. The equation says $u=f+\lambda c\,x$. Multiply by $y$, rename the variable and integrate: $c=\int_0^1yf(y)\,dy+\lambda c\int_0^1y^2\,dy$, that is,
$$c\Big(1-\frac\lambda3\Big)=\int_0^1yf(y)\,dy .$$
If $\lambda\ne3$ there is exactly one solution, $u(x)=f(x)+\dfrac{\lambda x}{1-\lambda/3}\displaystyle\int_0^1yf(y)\,dy$. For $\lambda=1$, $f\equiv1$: $c=\frac{1/2}{2/3}=\frac34$ and $u(x)=1+\frac34x$. Check: $\int_0^1y(1+\tfrac34y)\,dy=\tfrac12+\tfrac14=\tfrac34$, as required.

If $\lambda=3$, the equation is solvable only when $\int_0^1yf(y)\,dy=0$, and then $u=f+Cx$ for every constant $C$.

In the language of the theorem: the operator $(Tu)(x)=x\int_0^1yu(y)\,dy$ is compact (rank one) and self-adjoint (the kernel $xy$ is symmetric), with the single nonzero eigenvalue $\frac13$ and eigenvector $x$. The equation is $(T-\mu I)u=-\mu f$ with $\mu=1/\lambda$. For $\mu\ne\frac13$ the homogeneous equation has only $u=0$, so there is a unique solution. For $\mu=\frac13$ the kernel of $T^*-\mu I$ is spanned by $x$, and the solvability condition is $f\perp x$, exactly what we found.

blocks.title: The Volterra operator
blocks.body: Let $(Vu)(x)=\int_0^xu(t)\,dt$ on $L^2[0,1]$. Show that $V$ is compact, that it has no eigenvalues at all, and that $\|V\|=2/\pi$.
blocks.solution:
$V$ is the integral operator with kernel $K(x,t)=1$ for $t< x$ and $0$ otherwise, which is square-integrable, so $V$ is a Hilbert–Schmidt operator and hence compact.

Eigenvalues: suppose $Vu=\lambda u$. If $\lambda=0$, then $\int_0^xu=0$ for all $x$, so $u=0$ almost everywhere. If $\lambda\ne0$, then $u=\lambda^{-1}Vu$ is continuous, hence $Vu$ is $C^1$ and so is $u$, with $u'=u/\lambda$ and $u(0)=\lambda^{-1}(Vu)(0)=0$. The only solution is $u=0$. So $V$ has no eigenvalues, which is possible because $V$ is not self-adjoint. By the Fredholm alternative, $V-\lambda I$ is then invertible for every $\lambda\ne0$, so the spectrum of $V$ is $\{0\}$.

Norm: $\|V\|^2=\|V^*V\|$, and $V^*V$ is compact and self-adjoint, so $\|V\|^2$ is its largest eigenvalue. Here $(V^*u)(x)=\int_x^1u(t)\,dt$. Try $u(x)=\cos ax$ with $a=(2k-1)\pi/2$: $(Vu)(s)=\sin(as)/a$ and
$$(V^*Vu)(x)=\int_x^1\frac{\sin as}{a}\,ds=\frac{\cos ax-\cos a}{a^2}=\frac{\cos ax}{a^2},$$
since $\cos a=0$. These cosines form an orthonormal basis of $L^2[0,1]$ up to normalisation (they are the eigenfunctions of $-u''$ with $u'(0)=0$, $u(1)=0$), so the eigenvalues of $V^*V$ are $\frac{4}{(2k-1)^2\pi^2}$, the largest being $\frac4{\pi^2}$ at $k=1$. Hence $\|V\|=\frac2\pi\approx0.637$.

blocks.body:
- Compact is much stronger than bounded. The identity and every isometry of an infinite-dimensional space are bounded and not compact.
- The alternative is about $T-\lambda I$ with $\lambda\ne0$. For $\lambda=0$ it fails: $T$ itself is never invertible in infinite dimensions, and its range is typically not closed ($D$ with $\mu_n=1/n$ has dense, non-closed range).
- A compact operator need not have any eigenvalues (the Volterra operator). The spectral theorem needs self-adjointness, or at least normality.
- Compactness depends on the spaces. The inclusion of $C^1[0,1]$ into $C[0,1]$ is compact, but the identity of $C[0,1]$ is not; differentiation $C^1\to C$ is bounded but not compact.
- In the spectral expansion, $\sum\lambda_n\langle x,e_n\rangle e_n$ converges in norm for each $x$, and in operator norm as an operator series, but the $e_n$ alone span only the closure of the range; $\ker T$ may be infinite-dimensional.

The main applications are to differential equations. A regular [[sturm-liouville]] problem is inverted by an integral operator with a continuous symmetric Green's function; that operator is compact and self-adjoint, so the spectral theorem gives a complete orthonormal family of eigenfunctions, the abstract reason why [[fourier-series]] and separation of variables work for the [[heat-equation]] and [[wave-equation]]. For the Dirichlet problem for the [[laplace-equation]] on a bounded domain, the inverse of the Laplacian is compact on $L^2$ (by Rellich's compactness theorem for Sobolev spaces), which yields the discrete spectrum of a vibrating drum. In the Banach-space setting, $T-\lambda I$ with $T$ compact is the prototype of a Fredholm operator, whose index $\dim\ker-\operatorname{codim}\operatorname{ran}$ is stable under compact perturbations; this is the starting point of index theory. The page builds on [[hilbert-spaces]], [[spectral-theorem]] and [[arzela-ascoli]], and uses the norm-preserving extension of [[hahn-banach]] in the Banach-space version.

1. Show that if $T$ is compact and $(e_n)$ is an orthonormal sequence, then $Te_n\to0$ in norm.
2. For the kernel $K(x,y)=x+y$ on $[0,1]^2$, find the two nonzero eigenvalues of the integral operator and check that their sum is $\int_0^1K(x,x)\,dx$. For which $\lambda$ does $u-\lambda Ku=f$ fail to have a unique solution?
3. Show that the operator on $\ell^2$ given by $(Tx)_n=x_{n+1}/n$ is compact, and find its spectrum.
4. Prove that the inclusion map $C^1[0,1]\to C[0,1]$, with norms $\|u\|_\infty+\|u'\|_\infty$ and $\|u\|_\infty$, is compact.

sources.ref: Brezis, Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and Partial Differential Equations
Kreyszig, Introductory Functional Analysis with Applications
Reed & Simon, Methods of Modern Mathematical Physics I: Functional Analysis

entry.sum: The joint distribution of random variables $X$ and $Y$ describes how they behave together, through a joint probability mass function or density from which the individual (marginal) distributions are obtained by summing or integrating out the other variable. Covariance $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=E[XY]-E[X]E[Y]$ measures linear association and enters the variance of every linear combination; the conditional expectation $E[X\mid Y]$ is the best prediction of $X$ from $Y$, and averaging it recovers $E[X]$.
entry.why: Almost every real question involves more than one random quantity: total weights of several items, measurement plus noise, a stock and an index. Covariance controls the risk of sums and portfolios, and conditional expectation is the basis of prediction, regression and martingale theory.

links.note: In simple linear regression the least-squares slope is the sample covariance divided by the sample variance of the predictor, the sample version of the best linear predictor $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)/\operatorname{Var}X$.
The covariance matrix of a random vector is symmetric positive semidefinite, and diagonalising it by the spectral theorem is principal component analysis.

refs: Ross, A First Course in Probability
Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes
Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability

blocks.body:
Knowing the distribution of the height of a randomly chosen person, and separately the distribution of their weight, does not tell you how likely it is that someone is both tall and light. For that you need the joint distribution: a description of the pair. Questions about sums ("the total weight of six packets and a box"), predictions ("the expected weight given the height") and dependence ("do these move together?") are all questions about joint distributions.

This page assumes single [[random-variables]] and the standard [[distributions]], and uses double integrals from [[multiple-integrals]] for the continuous case. It builds three tools: joint and marginal distributions, covariance and correlation, and conditional expectation.

blocks.title: Joint distribution
blocks.body:
For random variables $X,Y$ on the same probability space, the joint distribution function is $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,\ Y\le y)$.

- Discrete case: the joint probability mass function is $p(x,y)=P(X=x,\ Y=y)$, and $P((X,Y)\in A)=\sum_{(x,y)\in A}p(x,y)$.
- Continuous case: $X,Y$ have joint density $f\ge0$ if $P((X,Y)\in A)=\iint_Af(x,y)\,dx\,dy$ for all (reasonable) regions $A$; then $\iint_{\mathbb{R}^2}f=1$.

The marginal distributions are recovered by summing or integrating out the other variable: $p_X(x)=\sum_yp(x,y)$ and $f_X(x)=\int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x,y)\,dy$. $X$ and $Y$ are independent if $p(x,y)=p_X(x)p_Y(y)$ for all $x,y$ (respectively $f(x,y)=f_X(x)f_Y(y)$). The expectation of a function of both is $E[g(X,Y)]=\sum g(x,y)\,p(x,y)$ or $\iint g\,f$.

Meaning: the joint distribution is the full description of the pair; the marginals are its shadows on the two axes, and different joint distributions can cast the same shadows.

blocks.title: A small table
Covariance and correlation
blocks.body:
For $X,Y$ with finite variances, with $\mu_X=E[X]$ and $\mu_Y=E[Y]$,
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=E\big[(X-\mu_X)(Y-\mu_Y)\big]=E[XY]-\mu_X\mu_Y,$$
and if both variances are positive the correlation is $\rho(X,Y)=\dfrac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y}$. Covariance is symmetric, bilinear ($$\operatorname{Cov}(aX+bZ,Y)=a\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)+b\operatorname{Cov}(Z,Y)$$), and $\operatorname{Cov}(X,X)=\operatorname{Var}X$. If $X$ and $Y$ are independent then $E[XY]=E[X]E[Y]$, so $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0$.

Meaning: covariance is positive when $X$ and $Y$ tend to be above their means together, negative when one tends to be above while the other is below; correlation is the scale-free version.

blocks.title: Variance of a linear combination, and the correlation bound
blocks.body:
For random variables $X,Y$ with finite variances and constants $a,b$,
$$\operatorname{Var}(aX+bY)=a^2\operatorname{Var}X+b^2\operatorname{Var}Y+2ab\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y).$$
In particular, for independent $X_1,\dots,X_n$, $\operatorname{Var}(X_1+\cdots+X_n)=\sum\operatorname{Var}X_i$. Moreover $-1\le\rho(X,Y)\le1$, with $|\rho|=1$ exactly when $Y=\alpha+\beta X$ with probability $1$ for some constants with $\beta\ne0$.

Put $\tilde X=X-\mu_X$ and $\tilde Y=Y-\mu_Y$. Then $aX+bY-E[aX+bY]=a\tilde X+b\tilde Y$, and expanding the square,
$$\operatorname{Var}(aX+bY)=E\big[a^2\tilde X^2+2ab\tilde X\tilde Y+b^2\tilde Y^2\big]=a^2\operatorname{Var}X+2ab\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)+b^2\operatorname{Var}Y,$$
by linearity of expectation. The statement for $n$ independent variables follows by induction, since all covariances vanish.

For the bound, apply the formula to the standardised variables $U=\tilde X/\sigma_X$ and $V=\tilde Y/\sigma_Y$, which have variance $1$ and covariance $\rho$:
$$0\le\operatorname{Var}(U\pm V)=2\pm2\rho .$$
So $-1\le\rho\le1$. If $\rho=1$ then $\operatorname{Var}(U-V)=0$, so $U-V$ is constant, and since $E[U-V]=0$ it is $0$ with probability $1$; that is, $Y=\mu_Y+\frac{\sigma_Y}{\sigma_X}(X-\mu_X)$. The case $\rho=-1$ is the same with $U+V$. (This is the [[cauchy-schwarz]] inequality for the inner product $E[\tilde X\tilde Y]$.)

blocks.title: Sums of independent random variables
blocks.body:
If $X$ and $Y$ are independent with densities $f_X,f_Y$, the density of $S=X+Y$ is the convolution
$$f_S(s)=\int_{-\infty}^\infty f_X(x)\,f_Y(s-x)\,dx,$$
obtained by integrating the joint density $f_X(x)f_Y(y)$ over the half-plane where $x+y\le s$ and differentiating in $s$. For example, if $X,Y$ are independent exponential with rate $\lambda$, then for $s>0$
$$f_S(s)=\int_0^s\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\,\lambda e^{-\lambda(s-x)}\,dx=\lambda^2s\,e^{-\lambda s},$$
a gamma density.

The most used case is the normal one. If $X\sim N(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)$ and $Y\sim N(\mu_2,\sigma_2^2)$ are independent, then
$$aX+bY\sim N\big(a\mu_1+b\mu_2,\ a^2\sigma_1^2+b^2\sigma_2^2\big).$$
The mean and variance follow from linearity and the theorem above; that the result is again normal can be proved from the convolution formula or, more quickly, with [[moment-generating]] functions. Independence is essential here; jointly normal variables with nonzero covariance add their covariance term as in the theorem.

A common trap is to confuse $X_1+X_2$ (two independent copies) with $2X$ (one copy doubled). Both have mean $2\mu$, but $\operatorname{Var}(X_1+X_2)=2\sigma^2$ while $\operatorname{Var}(2X)=4\sigma^2$: independent errors partly cancel, a doubled error does not.

blocks.title: Conditional distribution and conditional expectation
blocks.body:
In the discrete case, for $y$ with $p_Y(y)>0$, the conditional pmf of $X$ given $Y=y$ is $p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=p(x,y)/p_Y(y)$. In the continuous case, for $y$ with $f_Y(y)>0$, the conditional density is $f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=f(x,y)/f_Y(y)$. The conditional expectation of $X$ given $Y=y$ is the mean of this distribution,
$$m(y)=E[X\mid Y=y]=\sum_xx\,p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\quad\text{or}\quad\int x\,f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\,dx,$$
and $E[X\mid Y]$ denotes the random variable $m(Y)$.

Meaning: $E[X\mid Y]$ is your best guess of $X$ once you have seen $Y$; it is a function of $Y$, not a number.

blocks.title: Tower property and law of total variance
blocks.body:
If $E|X|< \infty$ then $E\big[E[X\mid Y]\big]=E[X]$. If moreover $E[X^2]< \infty$, then with $\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)=E[X^2\mid Y]-E[X\mid Y]^2$,
$$\operatorname{Var}X=E\big[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)\big]+\operatorname{Var}\big(E[X\mid Y]\big).$$

blocks.title: Proof (discrete case; the continuous case replaces sums by integrals)
blocks.body:
For the tower property,
$$E[m(Y)]=\sum_ym(y)\,p_Y(y)=\sum_y\sum_xx\,\frac{p(x,y)}{p_Y(y)}\,p_Y(y)=\sum_x x\sum_yp(x,y)=\sum_xx\,p_X(x)=E[X],$$
where swapping the order of summation is justified by absolute convergence. Applying the same identity to $X^2$ gives $E\big[E[X^2\mid Y]\big]=E[X^2]$. Then
$$E\big[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)\big]+\operatorname{Var}\big(m(Y)\big)=\Big(E[X^2]-E[m(Y)^2]\Big)+\Big(E[m(Y)^2]-E[m(Y)]^2\Big)=E[X^2]-E[X]^2 .$$

blocks.title: Conditional expectation as best prediction
blocks.body:
Why is $m(Y)=E[X\mid Y]$ the best guess? Assume $E[X^2]< \infty$. For any function $g$ with $E[g(Y)^2]< \infty$,
$$E\big[(X-g(Y))^2\big]=E\big[(X-m(Y))^2\big]+E\big[(m(Y)-g(Y))^2\big].$$
The cross term $2E\big[(X-m(Y))(m(Y)-g(Y))\big]$ vanishes: conditioning on $Y$, the factor $m(Y)-g(Y)$ is known, and $E[X-m(Y)\mid Y]=0$; then apply the tower property. So no function of $Y$ predicts $X$ with smaller mean squared error than $E[X\mid Y]$. Restricting $g$ to straight lines $g(y)=\alpha+\beta y$ gives instead the best linear predictor, with slope $\beta=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)/\operatorname{Var}Y$; its sample version is the least-squares line of [[linear-regression]]. Geometrically, $E[X\mid Y]$ is an orthogonal projection, which is how it is defined in general in measure-theoretic probability.

Joint densities also transform by the change-of-variables formula of [[multiple-integrals]]: if $(U,V)=\varphi(X,Y)$ with $\varphi$ smooth and invertible, then $f_{U,V}(u,v)=f_{X,Y}(\varphi^{-1}(u,v))\,\big|\det D\varphi^{-1}(u,v)\big|$. For example, if $X,Y$ are independent standard normal, in polar coordinates the joint density of $(R,\Theta)$ is $\frac1{2\pi}e^{-r^2/2}\,r$ for $r>0$, $0\le\theta<2\pi$. It factors, so $R$ and $\Theta$ are independent, $\Theta$ is uniform, and $P(R^2>t)=e^{-t/2}$. Read backwards, this is the Box–Muller method for generating normal samples from uniform ones (see [[monte-carlo]]).

blocks.title: Covariance from the table
blocks.body: For the made-up table above, compute $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$, $\rho(X,Y)$, and check the law of total variance.
blocks.solution:
The only nonzero products $xy$ come from $(1,1)$ and $(2,1)$, so $E[XY]=1\cdot0.1+2\cdot0.1=0.3$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0.3-1.1\cdot0.4=-0.14$. Next $E[X^2]=0.3+4\cdot0.4=1.9$, so $\operatorname{Var}X=1.9-1.21=0.69$, and $\operatorname{Var}Y=0.4\cdot0.6=0.24$. Hence
$$\rho=\frac{-0.14}{\sqrt{0.69\cdot0.24}}\approx-0.344 .$$
Large $X$ goes with $Y=0$ somewhat more often than independence would predict.

Total variance: given $Y=0$, $E[X^2\mid Y=0]=\frac13+4\cdot\frac12=\frac73$, so $\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y=0)=\frac73-\frac{16}9=\frac59$. Given $Y=1$, $E[X^2\mid Y=1]=\frac14+1=\frac54$, so $\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y=1)=\frac54-\frac9{16}=\frac{11}{16}$. Then $E[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)]=0.6\cdot\frac59+0.4\cdot\frac{11}{16}=\frac13+\frac{11}{40}=\frac{73}{120}$. The random variable $E[X\mid Y]$ takes the values $\frac43$ and $\frac34$ with probabilities $0.6$ and $0.4$ and has mean $1.1$, so its variance is $0.6\cdot\frac{16}9+0.4\cdot\frac9{16}-1.21=\frac{49}{600}$. The sum is $\frac{73}{120}+\frac{49}{600}=\frac{414}{600}=0.69=\operatorname{Var}X$.

blocks.title: A continuous joint density
blocks.body: Let $(X,Y)$ have density $f(x,y)=x+y$ on the unit square $0\le x,y\le1$ (and $0$ elsewhere). Find the marginals, $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$, $\rho$, and $E[Y\mid X=x]$.
blocks.solution:
First, $\int_0^1\!\int_0^1(x+y)\,dy\,dx=\frac12+\frac12=1$, so $f$ is a density. The marginal of $X$ is $f_X(x)=\int_0^1(x+y)\,dy=x+\frac12$, and by symmetry $f_Y(y)=y+\frac12$.

Moments: $E[X]=\int_0^1x(x+\frac12)\,dx=\frac13+\frac14=\frac7{12}$, $E[X^2]=\int_0^1x^2(x+\frac12)\,dx=\frac14+\frac16=\frac5{12}$, so $\operatorname{Var}X=\frac5{12}-\frac{49}{144}=\frac{11}{144}$, and the same for $Y$. Next $E[XY]=\int_0^1\!\int_0^1xy(x+y)\,dy\,dx=\frac16+\frac16=\frac13$. Hence
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\frac13-\frac{49}{144}=-\frac1{144},\qquad\rho=\frac{-1/144}{11/144}=-\frac1{11}.$$
Since the covariance is nonzero, $X$ and $Y$ are dependent (also visible from $f(x,y)\ne f_X(x)f_Y(y)$).

Conditional expectation: $f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=\dfrac{x+y}{x+\frac12}$ on $[0,1]$, so
$$E[Y\mid X=x]=\frac{\int_0^1y(x+y)\,dy}{x+\frac12}=\frac{\frac x2+\frac13}{x+\frac12}=\frac{3x+2}{6x+3}.$$
It decreases from $\frac23$ at $x=0$ to $\frac59$ at $x=1$, matching the negative correlation. Tower check: $\int_0^1\frac{3x+2}{6x+3}(x+\frac12)\,dx=\int_0^1\big(\frac x2+\frac13\big)dx=\frac14+\frac13=\frac7{12}=E[Y]$.

blocks.title: Packing to a weight limit
blocks.body: In a made-up packing model, a packet's weight is $N(500,4^2)$ grams and an empty box weighs $N(100,3^2)$ grams, all weights independent. A full box holds six packets. Find the probability that a full box weighs more than $3110$ grams. Compare with a careless model in which one packet's weight is multiplied by six.
blocks.solution:
Assumptions: the seven weights are independent and normally distributed. Then $W=X_1+\cdots+X_6+B$ is normal with mean $6\cdot500+100=3100$ and variance $6\cdot16+9=105$. So
$$P(W>3110)=1-\Phi\Big(\frac{10}{\sqrt{105}}\Big)=1-\Phi(0.9759)\approx0.165 .$$
The careless model $6X_1+B$ has the same mean but variance $36\cdot16+9=585$, giving $1-\Phi(10/\sqrt{585})=1-\Phi(0.413)\approx0.340$: about twice the true probability. Six independent packets average out; one packet copied six times does not.

blocks.title: Minimum and maximum of two random numbers
blocks.body: Choose $U_1,U_2$ independently and uniformly from $[0,1]$, and let $X=\min(U_1,U_2)$ and $Y=\max(U_1,U_2)$. Find the joint density of $(X,Y)$, $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$, $\rho(X,Y)$ and $E[X\mid Y]$.
blocks.solution:
The pair $(U_1,U_2)$ is uniform on the unit square, and $(X,Y)$ is obtained by folding the square along its diagonal: each point of the triangle $0\le x\le y\le1$ receives the density from two points of the square, $(x,y)$ and $(y,x)$. So $(X,Y)$ is uniform on that triangle, with density $f(x,y)=2$ there and $0$ elsewhere. The support is a triangle, not a rectangle, so $X$ and $Y$ cannot be independent.

Marginals: $f_X(x)=\int_x^12\,dy=2(1-x)$ and $f_Y(y)=\int_0^y2\,dx=2y$, so $E[X]=\frac13$ and $E[Y]=\frac23$. For $E[XY]$ there is a shortcut: $XY=U_1U_2$ always, so $E[XY]=E[U_1]E[U_2]=\frac14$. Thus $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\frac14-\frac29=\frac1{36}$. Also $E[X^2]=\int_0^12(1-x)x^2\,dx=\frac16$, so $\operatorname{Var}X=\frac16-\frac19=\frac1{18}$, and similarly $\operatorname{Var}Y=\frac12-\frac49=\frac1{18}$. Hence $\rho=\frac{1/36}{1/18}=\frac12$.

Given $Y=y$, the conditional density of $X$ is $2/(2y)=1/y$ on $[0,y]$: uniform. So $E[X\mid Y]=Y/2$, and the tower property gives $E[X]=E[Y]/2=\frac13$, as it should.

blocks.body:
- Uncorrelated does not mean independent. If $X$ is uniform on $\{-1,0,1\}$ and $Y=X^2$, then $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=E[X^3]-E[X]E[X^2]=0$, yet $Y$ is a function of $X$.
- The marginals do not determine the joint distribution. Two fair coins that are independent and two coins that always agree have the same marginals.
- $$\operatorname{Var}(X-Y)=\operatorname{Var}X+\operatorname{Var}Y-2\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$$. For independent variables variances add even when the variables are subtracted.
- Factorisation must hold on the whole plane, including the shape of the support: a density that is constant on a triangle is not a product of a function of $x$ and a function of $y$.
- Each of $X$ and $Y$ being normal does not make $aX+bY$ normal; that needs independence or joint normality.
- $E[X\mid Y]$ is a random variable (a function of $Y$), while $E[X\mid Y=y]$ is a number.

Covariance and conditional expectation are the raw material of much of probability and statistics. The [[limit-theorems]] use $\operatorname{Var}(\sum X_i)=\sum\operatorname{Var}X_i$ for independent variables, which is why averages concentrate at rate $1/\sqrt n$. [[moment-generating]] functions turn sums of independent variables into products. [[markov-chains]] are specified by conditional distributions of the next state given the present one. Best prediction by $E[X\mid Y]$ and the best linear predictor lead to [[linear-regression]]. The measure-theoretic version of conditional expectation, defined as a projection onto a sub-$\sigma$-algebra, is the foundation of [[martingales]], and [[monte-carlo]] methods use change of variables for joint densities to simulate from given distributions.

1. A fair die is rolled twice. Let $X$ be the first result and $Y$ the larger of the two. Write out the joint pmf and find $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$.
2. Let $(X,Y)$ have density $f(x,y)=6x$ on $0\le x\le y\le1$. Find the marginal of $Y$ and $E[X\mid Y=y]$.
3. Show that $\operatorname{Cov}(X+Y,X-Y)=\operatorname{Var}X-\operatorname{Var}Y$. When are $X+Y$ and $X-Y$ uncorrelated?
4. If $N$ is a nonnegative integer random variable independent of i.i.d. $X_1,X_2,\dots$ with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$, use the tower property and the law of total variance to find the mean and variance of $X_1+\cdots+X_N$.
